title: A Bride for the Son of Promise
summary: Abraham’s servant, guided through prayer and providence, finds Rebekah in Nahor’s city; she chooses to go, and becomes Isaac’s beloved wife.
historicalContext: The chapter follows Sarah’s burial at Machpelah. Isaac married at forty (25:20), so about three years have passed since his mother’s death, and Abraham is near one hundred and forty. Marriages in the ancient Near East were family arrangements: the groom’s household sought a bride, gifts were exchanged, and the bride’s kin gave consent, though the young woman’s own willingness could still be sought. Abraham’s relatives had remained in upper Mesopotamia, in Aram-naharaim, the region of the upper Euphrates and its tributaries, where texts from Mari name a town called Nahur near Haran. The journey of some five hundred miles by camel caravan would have taken weeks. Wells and springs outside a town were public gathering points where women drew water at evening. The household Abraham left still knew the LORD’s name, yet it also kept household gods (31:19, 30; Joshua 24:2), so the setting mixes remembered truth with idolatry.
literaryContext: Genesis 24 is the longest chapter in Genesis and closes the account of Abraham’s life before his death in 25:7–8. Its last words given to Abraham (vv. 6–8) confess faith in the promise of land and seed. The story moves from Abraham’s house in Canaan to the well of Nahor, into Bethuel’s household, back to a well in the Negeb, and finally into Sarah’s tent. God never speaks aloud in the chapter, yet the LORD is named again and again as the One who leads, prospers, and shows steadfast love; providence works through prayer, ordinary customs, and human choices. The servant’s retelling of events (vv. 34–49) is the chapter’s centre, and the small changes he makes show tact and faith. Rebekah’s “I will go” (v. 58) echoes Abraham’s own departure in 12:1–4, and the blessing spoken over her (v. 60) echoes the oath of 22:17. Isaac, received back from the altar on Moriah, now receives a bride, and the line of promise passes to a new generation.
themes: Providence that answers prayer through ordinary events
Covenant faithfulness: the LORD’s steadfast love and truth
Marriage within the faith of the promise
A faithful servant who puts his errand before himself
Rebekah’s free choice to leave home and follow
Succession of the promise from Abraham to Isaac

outline.title: Abraham Commissions His Servant
outline.summary: The aged Abraham binds his chief servant by oath to find Isaac a wife among his kindred, never among the Canaanites, and never to take Isaac back.

outline.title: Prayer and Answer at the Well
outline.summary: At the well of Nahor’s city the servant asks the LORD for a sign; Rebekah fulfils it, proves to be Abraham’s kin, and the servant worships.

outline.title: Welcome in Bethuel’s House
outline.summary: Rebekah runs home, Laban hurries out at the sight of the gold, and the servant refuses food until he has told his errand.

outline.title: The Servant Tells His Story
outline.summary: The servant recounts Abraham’s blessing, the oath, his prayer, and its answer, then asks the family to deal kindly and truly with his master.

outline.title: Consent, Delay, and Departure
outline.summary: The family confesses that the matter is from the LORD; when they try to delay, Rebekah says “I will go” and leaves with their blessing.

outline.title: Isaac Receives Rebekah
outline.summary: Isaac, walking in the field at evening, meets the caravan; Rebekah veils herself, becomes his wife in Sarah’s tent, and he loves her.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham was old, and well stricken in age: and the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter opens with two notes about Abraham. He “was old, and well stricken in age,” and “the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.” Isaac would marry at forty (25:20), so Abraham is about one hundred and forty, and Sarah has been in the grave at Machpelah for some three years. Age gives the scene its urgency. The promise of a multitude of descendants now hangs, humanly speaking, on an unmarried son, and the patriarch knows that his remaining strength is limited.

The second statement looks back over the whole story since Genesis 12. God had said, “I will bless thee” (12:2), and the narrator now records that the word has come true. Abraham’s wealth, his son, his safety among the nations, and even the burial plot he has just secured are evidence of the LORD’s favour. Blessing is the first and last word of this chapter’s opening and of its later speeches: the servant will repeat it to Rebekah’s family (v. 35), and they will bless Rebekah when she leaves (v. 60).

The blessing is not yet complete. The land is still mostly owned by others, and the nation is still one man. Abraham’s faith therefore looks forward, and his last recorded act is to secure the next step in God’s plan. God’s past faithfulness becomes the ground for trusting him with what remains.

Old age in Scripture is a time for passing on the faith as much as for resting from labour. The psalmist prays, “when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation” (Psalm 71:18). Abraham uses his remaining strength for that purpose. His concern in this chapter is not his own comfort or legacy but the continuation of God’s promise through his son.

wordNotes.term: בָּא בַּיָּמִים (ba bayyamim) — well stricken in age
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “gone into the days,” an idiom for advanced old age used of Abraham and Sarah in 18:11 and of Joshua and David near the end of their lives. It marks a time for settling the household’s future.

The verb of 12:2–3 returns as a completed fact: God has blessed Abraham “in all things.” In Genesis blessing includes life, fruitfulness, and prosperity given by God, and it is meant to flow on to others through Abraham’s seed.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham said unto his eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all that he had, Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham turns to “his eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all that he had.” The servant is never named in the chapter. Many have identified him with Eliezer of Damascus, the steward whom Abraham once expected to be his heir (15:2), and that identification fits his seniority and the trust placed in him, though the text leaves him anonymous. His namelessness keeps attention on his master, his God, and his mission. “Eldest” translates a word related to the “old” of verse 1; it points to rank as chief elder of the household as much as to age.

The man who manages everything Abraham owns is now asked to handle the most important matter of all. Abraham could have sent Isaac himself, or gone in person, but he chooses to entrust the task to a servant who shares his faith. The servant’s later prayers (vv. 12, 26–27, 52) show that Abraham’s teaching had shaped his household, as God intended when he said Abraham would command his children and his household after him (18:19).

The request “Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh” introduces a solemn oath. The same gesture appears only once more, when the dying Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (47:29). In both cases the oath concerns what is to happen after the one who imposes it has died, and in both the promise of the land is involved. “Thigh” is a reserved way of referring to the organ of procreation, the source of descendants (46:26; Exodus 1:5). Swearing at that place tied the oath to Abraham’s posterity, and so to the line through which the promised Seed would come. The precise meaning of the custom is uncertain, but its seriousness is plain.

wordNotes.term: עַבְדּוֹ זְקַן בֵּיתוֹ (avdo zeqan beito) — his eldest servant of his house
wordNotes.explanation: Zaqen, “old” or “elder,” here marks the servant’s standing as the senior officer of the household, one who “ruled over all.” The same root describes Abraham in verse 1, linking master and steward. The steward of a great household could act with full authority on his master’s behalf.

The word can denote the upper leg, but in phrases about descendants who “came out of” a man’s thigh it refers to the reproductive organs. Placing the hand there bound the oath to Abraham’s line and its future, possibly invoking the posterity in whom God’s promise rested.

verses.bibleText: And I will make thee swear by the LORD, the God of heaven, and the God of the earth, that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The oath is sworn “by the LORD, the God of heaven, and the God of the earth.” Abraham uses the covenant name, YHWH, and joins to it a title that recalls creation (1:1) and his earlier confession before Melchizedek and the king of Sodom of “the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth” (14:22). The God who rules both realms can direct events in a distant land as easily as in Canaan, and he will hold the servant to his word. The servant is about to leave Abraham’s presence, but he will never leave the presence of the God by whom he swore.

The heart of the oath is negative: “thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell.” Abraham has lived among the Canaanites for sixty years and has just negotiated courteously with the Hittites of Hebron (ch. 23). His objection is not to their persons. God had already said that the iniquity of the Amorites was moving toward its full measure (15:16), and Sodom had shown where Canaanite religion and morals were heading. A Canaanite wife would bring the gods and practices of the land into the household of promise. Abraham had seen how mixed loyalties brought grief through Hagar and through Lot’s family.

The concern is spiritual and covenantal. Later the law forbade Israel to give or take Canaanite marriage partners, “for they will turn away thy son from following me” (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). Esau’s Hittite wives became “a grief of mind” to Isaac and Rebekah (26:34–35), confirming Abraham’s judgment. The same principle reaches the church when Paul urges believers not to be “unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14). Faith is not inherited by birth into a family, and Abraham’s own kin were not free from idolatry, yet a home in which husband and wife share loyalty to the true God is the setting in which the promise could be taught to the next generation.

wordNotes.term: אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וֵאלֹהֵי הָאָרֶץ (Elohei hashamayim velohei ha’arets) — the God of heaven, and the God of the earth
wordNotes.explanation: A title that sets the LORD above every local deity. The phrase “God of heaven” becomes common later, especially when Israel lived among nations (Ezra 1:2; Jonah 1:9). Here it assures the servant that no region lies outside God’s rule.

wordNotes.term: וְאַשְׁבִּיעֲךָ (ve’ashbi‘akha) — and I will make thee swear
wordNotes.explanation: The causative form of the verb “to swear” means to put someone under oath. An oath in the name of the LORD invoked him as witness and judge of the promise, making the obligation sacred and binding even after the death of the one who imposed it.

verses.bibleText: But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son Isaac.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Positively, the servant is to “go unto my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son Isaac.” The words echo, in reverse, God’s call in 12:1: “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred.” Abraham left those places at God’s word; now his servant must go back to them, though not to settle. The movement will run in one direction only, from Mesopotamia to Canaan.

“My country” refers to the region of Haran in upper Mesopotamia, where Abraham’s brother Nahor’s family had settled (11:31; 22:20–23), not to Ur in the south. Abraham had received news of Nahor’s children and grandchildren, including Rebekah (22:23), so the choice of destination is informed. His relatives were not free from idolatry; Laban would later keep household images (31:19, 30), and Joshua recalls that Terah’s family “served other gods” (Joshua 24:2). Yet they still knew and used the LORD’s name (vv. 31, 50). A wife from among them was more likely to share Abraham’s faith than one raised in Canaanite worship.

The name Isaac appears here for the first time in the chapter, set at the end of the sentence for emphasis. Everything turns on this son, the child of promise through whom Abraham’s seed would be called (21:12). Securing his marriage is not merely family business; it is part of God’s purpose for the blessing of all nations.

Isaac himself says nothing in these opening verses. A man of about forty, he allows his father to direct the search for his wife, and he will accept the bride the servant brings. His willingness recalls his submission on Moriah, when he let himself be bound on the altar (22:9). In both scenes Isaac trusts his father and his father’s God, and in both he receives what God provides.

wordNotes.explanation: From the verb “to bear,” the word refers to one’s birthplace and wider family of origin. It is the same word God used when calling Abraham away from his kindred in 12:1. In verse 38 the servant substitutes “my father’s house” and “my family,” a closer circle.

verses.bibleText: And the servant said unto him, Peradventure the woman will not be willing to follow me unto this land: must I needs bring thy son again unto the land from whence thou camest?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Before swearing, the servant raises a practical objection: “Peradventure the woman will not be willing to follow me unto this land.” He is careful. An oath is binding, and he will not take it lightly or blindly. The question is realistic. A young woman would be asked to leave her family, travel hundreds of miles with a stranger, and marry a man she had never seen, in a land where her people had no standing.

His suggested alternative is that Isaac go back to Abraham’s homeland: “must I needs bring thy son again unto the land from whence thou camest?” From a human point of view the idea is sensible. If the bride cannot be brought to the groom, let the groom go to the bride. The servant is not doubting God; he is thinking through the terms of his obligation.

The question of the woman’s willingness becomes a thread through the whole chapter. Abraham will address it (v. 8), the servant will repeat it to the family (v. 39), and the story will reach its turning point when Rebekah herself is asked, “Wilt thou go with this man?” (v. 58). God’s leading does not override human choice; it works through it.

The servant’s question is also a model of honest commitment. Jesus urged those who would follow him to count the cost first, like a builder who sits down to reckon whether he can finish a tower (Luke 14:28–30). The servant asks before he swears, so that his oath will be one he can keep with a clear conscience.

wordNotes.explanation: “Perhaps,” expressing a real possibility. Abraham used the same word when interceding for Sodom (“Peradventure there be fifty righteous,” 18:24). The servant uses it again when retelling the story (v. 39).

wordNotes.term: הֶהָשֵׁב אָשִׁיב (hehashev ashiv) — must I needs bring … again
wordNotes.explanation: The doubled verb (infinitive plus finite form) adds emphasis: “Shall I really take your son back?” The verb shuv, “return,” becomes the key word of Abraham’s reply, which forbids any such return.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham said unto him, Beware thou that thou bring not my son thither again.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham’s answer is immediate and sharp: “Beware thou that thou bring not my son thither again.” On this point he will not negotiate. The servant may adapt in many ways, but Isaac must not go back to Mesopotamia, even to find a wife.

The reason lies in the call and the promise. God had brought Abraham out of that land and given Canaan to his seed (12:1, 7). To return would reverse the direction of faith. Abraham had learned from his own detours, into Egypt in famine (12:10–20) and into Gerar (ch. 20), that leaving the land on his own initiative led to trouble. There was also the danger that Isaac, once among his relatives, might be tempted to stay. Jacob later went to the same family and remained twenty years (31:38, 41).

Abraham never names the land he left; he calls it simply “thither,” there. Hebrews says of the patriarchs that if they had been mindful of the country from which they came out, “they might have had opportunity to have returned. But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Hebrews 11:15–16). Abraham’s refusal to let Isaac go back is an expression of that forward-looking faith. The promise lay ahead, in the land God had given, and ultimately in the city whose builder and maker is God.

His firmness also guards the next generation. A father’s decisions shape the path his children will walk, and Abraham does not leave Isaac’s future to convenience.

The warning also shows how settled Abraham’s faith had become. Decades earlier he had gone down to Egypt without asking God, and Lot had chosen the well-watered plain by sight. Now, near the end of his life, the old man will not trade the promise for convenience, even when convenience would solve a pressing family problem. Faith that has been tested learns to hold its ground.

wordNotes.explanation: “Guard yourself,” a strong warning used in the law when Israel is told not to forget the LORD or make covenants with the inhabitants of the land. Abraham treats taking Isaac back as a danger to be avoided at all costs.

verses.bibleText: The LORD God of heaven, which took me from my father's house, and from the land of my kindred, and which spake unto me, and that sware unto me, saying, Unto thy seed will I give this land; he shall send his angel before thee, and thou shalt take a wife unto my son from thence.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
These are Abraham’s last recorded words, and they are a confession of faith. He describes God as “the LORD God of heaven,” then recounts what this God has done: he “took me from my father’s house, and from the land of my kindred,” he “spake unto me,” and he “sware unto me, saying, Unto thy seed will I give this land.” The whole of Abraham’s story is summarised in three verbs: God took, God spoke, God swore. The oath he refers to is the one confirmed on Moriah after the binding of Isaac (22:16–18), where God swore by himself.

From this history Abraham draws a conclusion: “he shall send his angel before thee, and thou shalt take a wife unto my son from thence.” The God who called Abraham out of Mesopotamia will not now leave the promised seed without a wife. Abraham reasons from God’s promises to God’s provision. The same reasoning had sustained him on the mountain when he told Isaac, “God will provide himself a lamb” (22:8). The God who provided the ram will provide the bride.

“His angel” recalls the Angel of the LORD who called from heaven to stop Abraham’s hand (22:11, 15). That Angel speaks as God and swears in God’s name, and Scripture elsewhere presents him as a divine messenger who represents the LORD himself, the pre-incarnate Son. Here Abraham does not claim to have seen a vision; he simply trusts that the same heavenly Guide will go ahead of his servant. Israel would later receive the same promise as it journeyed toward Canaan: “I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way” (Exodus 23:20).

The chapter will never describe the angel appearing. His work will be seen only in timing, in a young woman’s generosity, and in a family’s consent. Hebrews speaks of angels as “ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). God’s guidance is often unseen, but it is no less real for that.

wordNotes.explanation: Mal’akh means “messenger,” human or heavenly. With the possessive “his,” it refers to a messenger sent by the LORD to guide and protect. In Genesis the Angel of the LORD speaks with divine authority (16:10; 22:11–12), and Exodus promises that God’s name is in him.

Abraham cites the land promise first given at Shechem (12:7). “Seed” is a collective noun for descendants that can also point to one individual. Paul notes this when he identifies the Seed of the promise with Christ (Galatians 3:16), the one in whom the inheritance is secured.

verses.bibleText: And if the woman will not be willing to follow thee, then thou shalt be clear from this my oath: only bring not my son thither again.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham answers the servant’s scruple directly: “if the woman will not be willing to follow thee, then thou shalt be clear from this my oath.” He is confident that God will provide, yet he does not presume to dictate how. If the woman refuses, the servant will not be held guilty. Faith trusts God’s promise without forcing God’s hand or making another person’s choice for them.

The release is generous, but one condition remains fixed: “only bring not my son thither again.” The repetition from verse 6 shows what matters most. A marriage could be sought elsewhere if necessary; a return to Mesopotamia could not be allowed.

Abraham’s words strike a balance found throughout Scripture. God’s purposes are certain, and he works to accomplish them, yet the people he calls remain free to accept or refuse. A woman who would not leave her family to join the household of promise would not be fit to bear its children. The servant is to invite, not to compel.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to be free, innocent, or exempt from an obligation or penalty. The spies use the same idea when telling Rahab they will be “blameless” of her oath if its terms are broken. The servant’s duty is to do his part faithfully, not to guarantee the result.

verses.bibleText: And the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and sware to him concerning that matter.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With his question answered, the servant takes the oath: he “put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and sware to him concerning that matter.” The narrator repeats the gesture of verse 2 and the swearing of verse 3, enclosing the conversation between the request and its fulfilment.

The servant swears only after he understands what he is promising. That order is wise. Scripture warns against rash vows (Ecclesiastes 5:2–5), and the servant’s caution in verse 5 was a sign of integrity, not reluctance. Once he has sworn, he does not hesitate again. From this point on he acts with the full weight of his master’s authority and with a solemn obligation before the LORD.

The phrase “Abraham his master” is the first of many times the servant is defined by his relationship to Abraham. His identity throughout the story is that of a man under orders, and his faithfulness to those orders becomes the way God’s providence is carried out.

The oath binds the servant even beyond Abraham’s lifetime. If the old man died while the servant was away, the obligation would still stand, for it was sworn before the LORD. That permanence explains why the gesture was reserved for promises reaching past death.

wordNotes.explanation: The simple passive-reflexive form of the verb means “bound himself by oath.” It completes the causative “I will make thee swear” of verse 3: Abraham imposed the oath, and the servant now takes it upon himself.

verses.bibleText: And the servant took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed; for all the goods of his master were in his hand: and he arose, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant sets out without delay. He “took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed.” Camels were costly and relatively few at this time; Abraham had acquired some in Egypt (12:16). A caravan of ten was an impressive sight and could carry supplies, gifts, and later the bride and her attendants (v. 61). The display of wealth would also serve as evidence of Abraham’s standing when the servant arrived (v. 35).

“For all the goods of his master were in his hand” explains how the servant could make such arrangements on his own authority. He was not a hired messenger but the steward of the whole estate, free to draw on its resources. The phrase may also mean that he took with him a selection of the best goods. Either way, Abraham trusted him completely, and the gifts he brought would later be given to Rebekah and her family (vv. 22, 53).

His destination was “Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor.” The Hebrew name is Aram-naharaim, the region of the upper Euphrates. The “city of Nahor” may be Haran, where Nahor’s family lived (27:43), or a nearby town named after him; tablets from Mari mention a town called Nahur in that region. The journey from the Negeb would have covered some five hundred miles and taken several weeks, yet the narrator passes over it in a single verse. The story’s interest lies not in distance but in what God does at the end of the road.

The servant’s promptness matches his master’s. When God told Abraham to offer Isaac, he “rose up early in the morning” and went (22:3). The servant likewise takes the oath and sets out without delay, carrying out a long and uncertain commission with the same readiness. Obedience in this household is not postponed until every question has been answered.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “Aram of the two rivers,” the land of the Arameans in upper Mesopotamia, between the Euphrates and its eastern tributaries. The Greek Old Testament rendered it “Mesopotamia,” “between the rivers,” which the KJV follows. Balaam and the oppressor Cushan-rishathaim came from the same region.

wordNotes.term: עִיר נָחוֹר (‘ir Nachor) — the city of Nahor
wordNotes.explanation: Either the city where Nahor lived or one bearing his name. Nahor was Abraham’s brother, whose family remained in the north (11:27–31). In 29:4–5 Jacob finds Nahor’s descendants at Haran, suggesting the two places were at least closely linked.

verses.bibleText: And he made his camels to kneel down without the city by a well of water at the time of the evening, even the time that women go out to draw water.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
On arrival the servant “made his camels to kneel down without the city by a well of water.” He does not go into the town and ask for Nahor’s house. He stops outside, at the place where the town’s life would come to him. The time is chosen as carefully as the place: “at the time of the evening, even the time that women go out to draw water.” Drawing water was women’s work, done in the cool of morning and evening (Exodus 2:16; 1 Samuel 9:11). A well was where a traveller could rest, gather news, and observe the young women of the town.

The servant is acting with practical wisdom. He positions himself where the right person is most likely to appear. Faith does not make him passive; it makes him thoughtful. He combines prudent planning with prayer, which he will offer in the next breath.

Wells are important meeting places in Genesis and beyond. Jacob will meet Rachel at a well in the same region (29:2–10), Moses will meet Zipporah at a well in Midian (Exodus 2:15–21), and Jesus will speak with a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well (John 4:6–7). The camels kneeling at evening, after a long day, set a scene of rest and expectation.

Nothing in this verse is miraculous. The servant uses the ordinary rhythms of village life, the evening walk of the women to the spring, as the setting in which he will look for God’s answer. Providence in Genesis rarely bypasses daily custom; it works within it, so that what happens at the well is both entirely natural and unmistakably directed.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּבְרֵךְ (vayyavrekh) — and he made … to kneel down
wordNotes.explanation: A rare causative use of the verb barakh, “kneel.” The same consonants form the common verb “to bless,” used of Abraham in verse 1. The words are homonyms rather than one idea, but the narrator may enjoy the sound: the caravan of the blessed man kneels at the place where God will show his favour.

verses.bibleText: And he said, O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant’s first act at the well is prayer: “O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham.” This is the first recorded prayer in Scripture in which someone asks God for specific guidance in a particular task. It is the prayer of a servant who has adopted his master’s God as his own. He addresses the LORD by his covenant name and identifies him by his relationship with Abraham, the God who had called, promised, and sworn.

“Send me good speed” renders a verb meaning “make it happen” or “cause it to meet me.” The same root describes Ruth’s arrival in Boaz’s field: “her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz” (Ruth 2:3). What looks like chance from a human angle is, in biblical thought, the arena of God’s rule. The servant asks God to arrange the meeting “this day,” here and now. His request is bold and specific, yet it springs from trust, not from presumption.

The basis of his prayer is God’s “kindness” to Abraham. The Hebrew word chesed is one of the richest in the Old Testament. It speaks of steadfast, loyal love that keeps covenant commitments and acts on behalf of those who depend on it. The servant does not ask for a favour on his own merits; he appeals to the LORD’s faithfulness to the promises made to Abraham. The word will recur at the high points of the story (vv. 14, 27, 49).

The servant’s prayer reflects the effect of Abraham’s household training. God had said that Abraham would “command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD” (18:19). Here a member of that household, far from home, turns first to God. His example shows how faith may be passed on through daily life and instruction to those who serve in a home. Prayer for guidance in the work God has given is never out of place; Jesus encouraged his disciples to ask, seek, and knock, assured that the Father gives good things to those who ask him (Matthew 7:7–11).

wordNotes.explanation: The causative of qarah, “to happen, meet,” means “cause to happen” or “bring about.” The servant asks God to direct what might seem a chance encounter. Nehemiah later uses a related request when he asks God to prosper him before the king.

Steadfast, covenant-keeping love: generous loyalty that goes beyond strict obligation. It is central to the LORD’s self-description in Exodus 34:6–7 and to the Psalms’ praise of his enduring mercy. In this chapter it describes God’s faithfulness to Abraham and, in verse 49, the response asked of Rebekah’s family.

verses.bibleText: Behold, I stand here by the well of water; and the daughters of the men of the city come out to draw water:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant describes his situation to God: “Behold, I stand here by the well of water; and the daughters of the men of the city come out to draw water.” He tells the LORD nothing the LORD does not already know, yet the description belongs to the prayer. It places the scene before God and acknowledges that he is now at the decisive point, surrounded by possibilities he cannot sort out on his own.

The young women are coming out as he prays. The moment is ripe, and he cannot tell which, if any, of them is the right one. His prayer is a confession of dependence. He has done everything prudence could suggest by choosing the place and the hour; the choice of the woman he leaves to God.

wordNotes.term: עֵין הַמָּיִם (‘ein hammayim) — the well of water
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Ayin usually means a spring, a natural source of flowing water, here probably with steps leading down (v. 16). The same word means “eye,” but in this phrase it simply describes the water source. Hagar was found by the angel “by a fountain of water” (16:7).

verses.bibleText: And let it come to pass, that the damsel to whom I shall say, Let down thy pitcher, I pray thee, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: let the same be she that thou hast appointed for thy servant Isaac; and thereby shall I know that thou hast shewed kindness unto my master.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant now proposes a sign: “let it come to pass, that the damsel to whom I shall say, Let down thy pitcher, I pray thee, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: let the same be she that thou hast appointed for thy servant Isaac.” The request itself is modest, a drink for a weary traveller. The answer he looks for is extraordinary: a young woman who, without being asked, offers to water ten camels.

The test is not arbitrary. A thirsty camel can drink many gallons, and ten camels after a long desert journey would need a great quantity of water, drawn by hand and carried up from the spring. Only a woman of unusual kindness, energy, and generosity would volunteer for such labour on behalf of a stranger. The sign would reveal character: hospitality to the traveller, care for animals, readiness to serve beyond what was asked. These were the qualities fitting for the wife of the son of Abraham, whose own hospitality had welcomed strangers at Mamre (18:1–8). Unlike Gideon’s fleece (Judges 6:36–40), the servant’s sign asks God to work through the natural expression of someone’s heart.

The servant speaks of the woman “thou hast appointed for thy servant Isaac.” He believes that God has already chosen a wife for Isaac and that his task is to discover her. He also calls Isaac God’s “servant,” recognising that the heir belongs to the LORD. The success of the sign will show “that thou hast shewed kindness unto my master.” He sees the answer to his prayer as evidence of God’s covenant love to Abraham.

This prayer is sometimes taken as a pattern for seeking signs in every decision. The setting suggests more caution. The servant was engaged in a task tied to God’s covenant purpose, he asked for a sign that tested moral qualities, and he remained ready to observe carefully before concluding anything (v. 21). Scripture commends asking God for wisdom (James 1:5) and acknowledging him in all our ways (Proverbs 3:5–6), but it does not authorise putting God to the test with demands for omens.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb yakach usually means to decide, judge, or reprove. Here it means to designate after weighing: God has determined who is right for Isaac. The servant repeats the word in verse 44. The same verb can describe God’s fair judgment between parties (31:42).

A young woman of marriageable age. In the consonantal text of the Pentateuch the word is often written like the masculine na‘ar, “youth,” but read as feminine. It refers to age and status rather than to moral character, which verse 16 describes separately.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, before he had done speaking, that, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The answer comes immediately: “before he had done speaking, that, behold, Rebekah came out.” The servant’s words are still on his lips when the woman appears. Isaiah records God’s promise, “before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear” (Isaiah 65:24), and Gabriel arrived while Daniel was still praying (Daniel 9:20–23). God had been arranging this meeting long before the servant arrived. Rebekah left her home in time to reach the well while he was praying.

The narrator introduces Rebekah with her genealogy: she “was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother.” The reader learns at once what the servant does not yet know. She is the granddaughter of Abraham’s brother, exactly the kindred Abraham had specified. Her descent through Milcah, Nahor’s wife, rather than through his concubine Reumah (22:24), marks her as a full member of the family. The genealogy of 22:20–23 had already prepared readers for her name.

She comes “with her pitcher upon her shoulder,” the posture of the servant’s prayer. The word “behold” draws the reader into the servant’s surprise. Everything is in place, but the test has not yet been made. The suspense of the following verses lies in whether this young woman will say and do what the servant asked.

The verse also shows how God’s timing and human freedom fit together. Rebekah came to the spring on her own errand, as she did every evening, carrying her own jar. No voice told her to go. Yet her ordinary choice to fetch water at that hour placed her where God’s purpose required. The servant’s prayer and her routine meet at the same moment.

wordNotes.explanation: A particle that directs attention to something sudden or significant, often presenting events from a character’s point of view. It marks Rebekah’s arrival here, the arrival of the camels in verse 63, and the ram caught in the thicket in 22:13.

The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some connect it with a word for a tether or cord, others with a stall-fed animal, but such derivations do not explain her role. Her character is revealed through her actions, not through an etymology.

verses.bibleText: And the damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: and she went down to the well, and filled her pitcher, and came up.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah is described with three phrases. She “was very fair to look upon,” like Sarah before her (12:11) and Rachel after her (29:17). She was “a virgin,” and the narrator adds, “neither had any man known her.” The second phrase confirms the first; the first word could simply describe a young woman of marriageable age, but the addition makes her purity explicit. The mother of the promised line must be a woman whose children would unquestionably be Isaac’s.

Scripture does not despise beauty, but it never treats it as the decisive qualification. The servant did not ask God for a beautiful woman; he asked for one with a generous heart. Proverbs says, “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30), and Peter commends the adorning of “a meek and quiet spirit” (1 Peter 3:3–4).

Then comes action: “she went down to the well, and filled her pitcher, and came up.” The spring lay below the town, reached by steps or a slope. The three verbs show her doing her ordinary task efficiently. She has not yet noticed the stranger. The servant watches and then makes his move.

The narrator’s description is given to the reader, not spoken to the servant. He has not yet learned her name or family, and he will judge her by what she does, not by how she looks. The order of the story makes that point plain: beauty is noted, but the test of character still lies ahead.

wordNotes.explanation: The word usually refers to a young woman who has not married and is of marriageable age. Its emphasis can fall on age and status, so the narrator adds “neither had any man known her” to state her chastity plainly. Laws in Deuteronomy assume the same sense of virginity.

wordNotes.term: טֹבַת מַרְאֶה (tovat mar’eh) — fair to look upon
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “good of appearance.” The same description returns for Rebekah in 26:7 and is applied to Bathsheba and Esther. Biblical narrative mentions beauty without moralising, but each story shows that character and God’s choice matter more.

verses.bibleText: And the servant ran to meet her, and said, Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
As soon as Rebekah comes up from the spring, “the servant ran to meet her.” The old steward does not wait for her to pass. His running shows eagerness; something about her has caught his attention, and he wants to put his test into effect at once. Running is a mark of eager service and hospitality in these chapters. Abraham ran to meet his visitors at Mamre (18:2, 7), Rebekah will run to water the camels (v. 20) and to tell her family (v. 28), and Laban will run out to the well (v. 29), though from different motives.

His request is deliberately small: “Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher.” He does not ask for help with his camels or for lodging, and he speaks courteously, with the polite particle “I pray thee.” The modesty of the request leaves room for her to reveal what is in her heart. Anyone might give a stranger a sip; what she does next, unprompted, will decide the matter.

The scene of a weary traveller asking a woman for water at a well invites comparison with Jesus at Sychar, who said to the Samaritan woman, “Give me to drink” (John 4:7). In both cases a simple request for water opens a conversation that leads to something much larger than thirst.

The servant’s request also required humility. A man in charge of a great estate, with ten camels and gold in his packs, asks a young woman for a sip from her jar. He puts himself in the position of one who receives. The test could only work if he asked as a dependent stranger rather than as a wealthy envoy.

wordNotes.term: הַגְמִיאִינִי נָא (hagmi’ini na’) — let me … drink a little
wordNotes.explanation: A rare causative verb meaning “let me swallow” or “give me a sip.” Together with “a little water,” it stresses how small the request was. The generosity of Rebekah’s response stands out against it.

verses.bibleText: And she said, Drink, my lord: and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah answers, “Drink, my lord.” She addresses the stranger with respect, calling him “my lord,” the ordinary courteous address to a man of standing. Her reply is warm and immediate. There is no suspicion or reluctance in it.

Then “she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink.” She lowers the heavy jar from her shoulder to her hand so that he can drink from it directly. The verb “hasted” will be repeated in verse 20. Abraham had “hastened” to prepare food for his visitors (18:6–7); Rebekah shows the same readiness to serve. She treats a stranger as an honoured guest without knowing who he is.

The servant’s first condition has been met. He asked her to let down her pitcher, and she has done so. The second and harder part of the sign is still to come. The narrator slows the action here, giving each movement a phrase, so that the reader shares the servant’s suspense as he waits to see whether she will offer more.

Rebekah’s courtesy illustrates the hospitality that Scripture repeatedly honours. “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers,” says Hebrews, “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2). She did not know she was serving the messenger of her future husband.

wordNotes.explanation: A respectful address to a superior or honoured stranger, comparable to “sir.” Sarah used the related word of Abraham (18:12), and Peter cites it as an example of respect (1 Peter 3:6). The servant also calls Abraham “my lord,” translated “my master.”

The verb means to act quickly, often from eagerness. It is used repeatedly of Abraham’s preparations for his guests in 18:6–7 and returns in verses 20 and 46. Rebekah’s speed shows willing service rather than grudging duty.

verses.bibleText: And when she had done giving him drink, she said, I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
When the servant has finished drinking, Rebekah speaks again: “I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking.” She volunteers what he had silently asked God for. No one had suggested it to her, and custom did not require it. It was a free expression of her character, and only so could it serve as a true answer to the prayer.

The offer is costly. Ten camels after a long journey might drink a great volume of water, each one needing many trips to the spring. Rebekah does not offer a token gesture; she commits herself to the whole task, “until they have done drinking.” Her words exceed the servant’s request. He had prayed only that she would offer to water the camels. She promises to keep going until every animal is satisfied.

God answered the servant’s prayer through a young woman’s natural generosity. Nothing supernatural happened at the well. Rebekah was simply the kind of person who sees a need and meets it. Providence did not override her freedom; it brought her, as she was, to the right place at the right moment. This is one of the clearest pictures in Scripture of how God often works: through ordinary people doing ordinary things with good hearts, in circumstances he has arranged.

Her conduct also reflects the kind of kindness to animals that Scripture commends. “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast” (Proverbs 12:10). Rebekah’s concern for the camels is part of her goodness, not an afterthought.

wordNotes.term: עַד אִם־כִּלּוּ לִשְׁתֹּת (‘ad ’im-killu lishtot) — until they have done drinking
wordNotes.explanation: The verb kalah means to finish or complete. Rebekah sets the end point of her labour not by her own strength but by the animals’ need. The same verb describes the servant finishing his drink and, in verse 22, the camels finishing theirs.

verses.bibleText: And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah does as she said: “she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels.” The narrator piles up verbs of action. She hurries, she empties, she runs, she draws. Each trip meant going down to the spring, filling the jar, climbing back, and emptying it into the stone trough beside the well, then going down again. The work would have taken a long time, perhaps hours, and she did it all.

The phrase “for all his camels” underlines that she did not stop halfway. She kept her word fully. Her energy matches her generosity; she is strong, industrious, and willing. These are exactly the qualities a household on the move, living in tents with flocks and herds, would need in its future mistress.

The parallels with Abraham’s hospitality in Genesis 18 are striking. Abraham ran, hastened, and brought a little water to wash his guests’ feet; Rebekah runs, hastens, and gives water to a stranger and his animals. The narrator suggests that she already shares the spirit of the household she is about to enter, even before she has heard of it.

Jesus taught that service rendered to the least, even “a cup of cold water,” is seen by God and not forgotten (Matthew 10:42). Rebekah’s labour at the trough brought her far more than she imagined: a place in the line of promise.

The narrator mentions no help from the servant’s men, and none is asked. Rebekah’s labour is entirely voluntary. Her willingness to work hard for others, with no promise of reward, reflects the character of the woman of strength in Proverbs, who “worketh willingly with her hands” and “stretcheth out her hand to the poor” (Proverbs 31:13, 20).

wordNotes.explanation: A watering trough for animals, related to the verb “to give drink.” The same kind of trough appears in Jacob’s breeding scheme and in Moses’ meeting with Jethro’s daughters, where shepherds water their flocks from it.

The verb means to pour out or lay bare. Rebekah tips the whole jar into the trough. The same verb appears in Isaiah 53:12, where the Servant “poured out his soul unto death,” a much weightier use of the image of emptying oneself.

verses.bibleText: And the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
While Rebekah works, the servant watches: “the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not.” He is astonished at what he sees. His prayer is being answered before his eyes, yet he does not leap to a conclusion. He stands silent, observing every detail, waiting until he is sure.

The silence shows both wonder and prudence. He has seen the sign fulfilled, but he does not yet know her family. Abraham had told him to take a wife from his kindred, and a kind young woman who was not of that kindred would not meet the terms of his oath. Faith does not make him careless. He gives God room to confirm what he has begun to see.

His reaction resembles that of the believers praying for Peter, who could hardly believe it when Peter, freed by an angel, stood knocking at the door (Acts 12:12–16). Even those who pray in faith are often surprised when God answers so promptly and so exactly.

The servant does not help with the camels. He lets Rebekah complete the task alone, perhaps because helping would have spoiled the test. The narrator is concerned to show that the answer came entirely through her free kindness.

The question “whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous or not” uses a word that will recur at the end of the episode (vv. 40, 42, 56). Success, for the servant, is not good luck or personal achievement but the LORD’s doing. He watches to learn what God has done, not to calculate what he can arrange.

wordNotes.explanation: A rare reflexive form, probably meaning “gazing intently” or “staring in amazement.” It conveys both astonishment and careful attention. The servant is caught between wonder at the answer and the need to confirm it.

The causative of tsalach, “to succeed,” means to bring to a successful end. God is the subject: he gives success. The same word describes the LORD prospering Joseph in Egypt and the blessing on the one who delights in God’s law.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
When the camels have finished drinking, the servant brings out his gifts: “a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold.” The “earring” is a nose ring, as verse 47 makes clear, an ornament worn in the side of the nose. A half shekel, or beka, weighed about a fifth of an ounce, and ten shekels of gold about four ounces. These were valuable gifts, far beyond any ordinary reward for watering camels.

The order of events raises a question. Here the servant gives the gifts before asking about her family (v. 23), but in his retelling he asks first and gives afterward (v. 47). The simplest explanation is that he brought the jewellery out and showed or offered it here, then presented it once her answer confirmed his hope. Alternatively, his confidence in God’s answer was so strong that he acted before the final confirmation, and when retelling he arranged the events in the order most likely to reassure her family. Either way, the gifts express gratitude, honour, and the hope that she was the one.

The value of the gifts signals that something more than courtesy is at stake. Gifts of jewellery were part of betrothal customs in that world, and Rebekah would have understood that the stranger was no ordinary traveller. Later, when her brother sees the gold, he hurries out to the well (v. 30).

The servant’s generosity reflects his master’s wealth, but also the abundance of God’s blessing on Abraham (v. 1). The gifts become a sign that the household of promise is able to provide for her. In Ezekiel 16:11–12 the LORD describes adorning Jerusalem as his bride with bracelets and a nose ring, using the same imagery of a bridegroom’s gifts.

wordNotes.explanation: A ring worn in the nose or ear. Verse 47 says the servant put it “upon her face,” and Isaiah lists “nose jewels” among the ornaments of Jerusalem’s women. The KJV’s “earring” is possible elsewhere, but here a nose ring is meant.

The word means “a split” or “half,” referring to half a shekel by weight. It was the amount each Israelite later gave for the sanctuary when numbered. Weights such as this have been found at archaeological sites, each about six grams.

verses.bibleText: And said, Whose daughter art thou? tell me, I pray thee: is there room in thy father's house for us to lodge in?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant asks two questions: “Whose daughter art thou? tell me, I pray thee: is there room in thy father’s house for us to lodge in?” The first is the decisive one. Rebekah has passed the test of character; now the servant needs to know whether she meets the condition of kinship. Everything depends on her answer.

The second question is a natural request for a traveller at evening. It also opens the way to her family, where the real business must be done. The servant cannot arrange a marriage at a well; he must speak with her father and her household. By asking for lodging he takes the next step toward that conversation.

His courtesy continues. He again uses the polite “I pray thee,” and he asks rather than demands. He is a guest in a foreign town, dependent on the hospitality of strangers, and he behaves accordingly. His conduct throughout the story combines confidence in God with respect for the people he meets.

The two questions also reveal the servant’s hope. He asks about her father’s house before he knows whether it is the house he seeks. If she is of Abraham’s kindred, the lodging will become the place where his errand is accomplished; if not, he will still need shelter and can continue his search. Either way, he takes the next practical step while waiting on God.

wordNotes.term: בַּת־מִי אַתְּ (bat-mi ’at) — whose daughter art thou?
wordNotes.explanation: Identity in the ancient world was established by family. The question seeks her father’s name and therefore her clan. Boaz asks a similar question about Ruth, and Saul asks whose son David is.
The verb lun means to pass the night. The angels at Sodom used it when they proposed to stay in the street (19:2). The servant asks for one night’s shelter; he will soon ask for much more.

verses.bibleText: And she said unto him, I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, which she bare unto Nahor.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah answers, “I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, which she bare unto Nahor.” The servant hears the names he has been longing for. Nahor was Abraham’s brother, and Bethuel was Nahor’s son by his wife Milcah. Rebekah is therefore Isaac’s first cousin once removed, a member of Abraham’s own kindred. God has led the servant not merely to the right town but to the right family and the right young woman.

Rebekah traces her descent through her grandmother Milcah. The mention matters because Nahor had children by a concubine as well (22:24). Rebekah belongs to the principal line of his family. The repeated naming of Milcah in this chapter (vv. 15, 24, 47) also shows the importance of mothers in these genealogies. Sarah, Milcah, and Rebekah each have a place in the story of the promised line.

The servant has not told her who he is. She answers a stranger’s question, unaware of the significance her words carry for him. For the reader, who already knows her lineage from verse 15, the drama lies in watching the servant learn what God has done.

This moment illustrates how God’s guidance often becomes clear only step by step. The servant prayed, watched, and asked. Each answer confirmed the last. The certainty he gained came through patient attention to what God was revealing.

Rebekah does not yet know that her answer will change her life. She simply tells the truth about her family. God often uses plain answers to ordinary questions to bring his purposes to light, and those who give them seldom realise at the time how much depends on what they say.

wordNotes.explanation: Nahor’s eighth son by Milcah and the father of Rebekah and Laban. The name probably contains the element ’el, “God,” though its exact meaning is uncertain. Bethuel remains in the background of the story, appearing only briefly in verse 50.

verses.bibleText: She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah adds, “We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in.” The servant asked only about room for the night; she answers for the camels too. Her generosity at the well continues in her invitation. She does not hesitate or say she must first ask her father. The household was evidently accustomed to hospitality, and she speaks with confidence that a traveller will be welcomed.

Her words complete the servant’s assurance. She has shown kindness, she belongs to Abraham’s family, and she has opened the door to her father’s house. Every obstacle he could have imagined at the start of his journey has been removed in the space of an evening. Before he says anything further to her, he turns to God.

wordNotes.term: תֶּבֶן וּמִסְפּוֹא (teven umispo’) — straw and provender
wordNotes.explanation: Teven is chopped straw used as bedding and fodder; mispo’ is animal feed in general. Both words reappear when the servant’s camels are cared for (v. 32) and when Joseph’s brothers feed their asses on the road home from Egypt.

verses.bibleText: And the man bowed down his head, and worshipped the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the man bowed down his head, and worshipped the LORD.” The servant’s first response to the answer is worship. He does not congratulate himself on his plan, nor does he immediately thank Rebekah. He bows before the God who has led him. The order is telling: gratitude to God comes before anything else.

The two verbs describe outward posture and inward devotion. He lowers his head, then bows himself in reverence, perhaps to the ground. This happens in front of Rebekah, at a public well, in a foreign town. His faith is not private embarrassment; it shapes his conduct openly. Rebekah would have seen a stranger worshipping the LORD at her family’s well, and that sight must have helped prepare her for what followed.

The servant’s worship frames the scene at the well. He began with prayer (v. 12) and ends with praise (v. 27). Between the two lies the whole sequence of God’s answer. Prayer and thanksgiving belong together. Many ask God for help but forget to return thanks when it comes; in Luke 17:15–18 only one of ten healed lepers came back to give glory to God. The servant is like that one. His example shows the fruit of a household in which the true God was honoured, for he had learned to worship from his master, who built altars wherever he went (12:7–8; 13:18).

Worship also guarded the servant against pride. A man who had planned his approach so carefully could easily have congratulated himself on his own wisdom. By bowing at once, he acknowledged that the plan had succeeded only because God had answered.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקֹּד וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ (vayyiqqod vayyishtachu) — and he bowed down his head, and worshipped
wordNotes.explanation: Qadad means to bow the head; the second verb means to prostrate oneself in homage. The pair often occurs together in moments of grateful worship, as when Israel heard of God’s concern for them in Egypt and when Moses saw the LORD’s glory pass by.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my master's brethren.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant puts his worship into words: “Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth.” To bless God is to acknowledge and praise what he has done. Noah had blessed “the LORD God of Shem” (9:26), and Melchizedek had blessed “the most high God” after Abraham’s victory (14:20); now a servant of Abraham’s household does the same beside a well in Mesopotamia, in thanks for an answered prayer.

His praise focuses on two qualities of God: “his mercy and his truth.” The first is chesed, the loyal, steadfast love the servant had asked God to show (vv. 12, 14). The second, emet, means faithfulness, reliability, trustworthiness. Together the two words describe God’s covenant character, and they often appear side by side in the Old Testament. When the LORD proclaimed his name to Moses, he described himself as “abundant in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). John says that grace and truth came by Jesus Christ (John 1:14, 17), using words that echo this pairing. The servant has discovered that God has not abandoned Abraham. The promises remain in force, and God is actively keeping them.

Then he adds a personal testimony: “I being in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my master’s brethren.” The Hebrew places “I” first for emphasis: as for me, while I was on the road, the LORD guided me. He had travelled hundreds of miles without knowing where exactly he was going, and God brought him to the very doorstep of Abraham’s relatives. The word for “led” is used elsewhere of God guiding his people, as a shepherd leads his flock (Psalm 23:3) and as the pillar of cloud led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21).

The phrase “in the way” is worth noting. God’s guidance came to the servant while he was moving in obedience. He did not sit at home waiting for a sign; he set out under orders and found God leading at each step. Guidance is often given to those who are already walking in the path of duty. As the psalmist says, “The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD” (Psalm 37:23).

The servant’s words also show that he is thinking of his master, not of himself. He rejoices because God has been faithful to Abraham. His success matters to him because it serves his master’s interests and God’s purpose.

wordNotes.term: חַסְדּוֹ וַאֲמִתּוֹ (chasdo va’amitto) — his mercy and his truth
wordNotes.explanation: Chesed is God’s loyal love; emet is his faithfulness, the quality of being firm and dependable. Paired, they describe God’s commitment to his promises, often meaning “faithful love.” Jacob uses the same pair in 32:10, and the Psalms celebrate them as going before God’s face. The servant will ask Rebekah’s family to show the same two qualities (v. 49).

The verb nachah means to lead or guide, frequently with God as subject, guiding his people on a journey. It is used of the pillar of cloud, of the shepherd’s guidance in Psalm 23, and of God leading in paths of righteousness.

verses.bibleText: And the damsel ran, and told them of her mother's house these things.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the damsel ran, and told them of her mother’s house these things.” Rebekah runs again, as she ran to water the camels. She is excited and eager to share what has happened: a stranger with ten camels, valuable gifts, a request for lodging, and a prayer of praise to the LORD God of Abraham, her great-uncle. She would have guessed that something important was afoot.

She goes to “her mother’s house” rather than her father’s. The expression likely refers to the women’s quarters within the household, where a young woman would naturally go first to tell her mother. The same phrase appears in Ruth 1:8 and the Song of Solomon in contexts dealing with a young woman’s family and marriage. It may also reflect the fact that Bethuel is strangely in the background throughout this story, perhaps because of age or weakness. Whatever the reason, the mother and the brother will take the leading roles in what follows (vv. 53, 55).

The phrase also anticipates the chapter’s ending. Rebekah leaves “her mother’s house” in Nahor’s city and is brought into “his mother Sarah’s tent” in Canaan (v. 67). The movement from one mother’s dwelling to another marks her passage from her old life into the household of promise.

Rebekah tells “these things,” all that had happened at the well: the stranger’s request, her offer, the gifts, and his words of praise. She becomes the first to carry the news, and her report sets the household in motion. Laban’s reaction in the next verses shows how differently the same news could be received.

wordNotes.explanation: An unusual phrase in a patriarchal setting, which normally speaks of the “father’s house.” It appears where a young woman’s family and marriage prospects are in view. Here it may refer to the women’s part of the household, where Rebekah would first report what had happened.

verses.bibleText: And Rebekah had a brother, and his name was Laban: and Laban ran out unto the man, unto the well.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Rebekah had a brother, and his name was Laban.” With these words the narrator introduces a man who will play a major role in the story of Jacob. Laban will later become Jacob’s father-in-law and employer, and his dealings with Jacob will be marked by cunning, broken agreements, and constant concern for his own advantage (29:15–30; 31:7, 41). The reader meets him here for the first time.

“Laban ran out unto the man, unto the well.” Like Rebekah, he runs. But the narrator will immediately explain what set him in motion (v. 30), and the explanation casts a shadow over his eagerness. Rebekah ran to serve; Laban runs because of what he has seen.

Laban’s name means “white,” which may suggest a fair complexion. The same word is used poetically for the moon (Isaiah 24:23), and some have connected the name with the moon worship known in Haran, though such a link cannot be proved. What is clear is that Laban’s household mixed knowledge of the LORD with other gods; Rachel would later steal his household idols (31:19, 30–35).

Laban takes charge as head of the family in negotiations, even though his father Bethuel is still alive (v. 50). Brothers in that culture had a recognised role in protecting and arranging marriages for their sisters, as Dinah’s brothers show (34:5–17). His prominence here also prepares for his later dominance in the household when Jacob arrives.

wordNotes.explanation: The name means “white.” The feminine form levanah is a poetic word for the moon. Whether or not the name reflects religious associations, Laban’s later actions, including keeping household gods, show a man whose loyalty to the LORD was mixed with other interests.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister's hands, and when he heard the words of Rebekah his sister, saying, Thus spake the man unto me; that he came unto the man; and, behold, he stood by the camels at the well.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator explains Laban’s haste: “when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister’s hands, and when he heard the words of Rebekah his sister, saying, Thus spake the man unto me; that he came unto the man.” The sentence puts the seeing before the hearing. Laban notices the gold first, then listens to his sister’s account. The narrator does not comment directly, but the order of the clauses invites the reader to draw a conclusion about what moved him most.

Laban’s later history confirms the suspicion. When Jacob arrived years later with nothing but a staff, Laban ran to meet him too (29:13), but when he found Jacob empty-handed he soon put him to work for wages, changed those wages ten times (31:7), and deceived him in marriage (29:25). A man whose eyes go first to gold will treat people according to what they bring.

The narrator adds, “and, behold, he stood by the camels at the well.” The servant has not moved. He waits patiently where Rebekah left him, beside his animals. He does not follow her into the town uninvited. His patience contrasts with Laban’s haste.

The verse illustrates how the same outward action can spring from different motives. Rebekah and Laban both run, both show hospitality, and both speak warmly to the stranger. One acts from generosity, the other from self-interest. Jesus warned, “Take heed, and beware of covetousness” (Luke 12:15), and Paul called the love of money a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:10). Laban’s welcome is real, but it is not pure.

wordNotes.explanation: Tsamid comes from a verb meaning “to bind” or “fasten,” referring to bands worn on the arms or wrists. The same word describes bracelets given to the sanctuary from Israel’s spoils and the ornaments God put on Jerusalem in Ezekiel’s parable.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Come in, thou blessed of the LORD; wherefore standest thou without? for I have prepared the house, and room for the camels.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban greets the servant: “Come in, thou blessed of the LORD; wherefore standest thou without? for I have prepared the house, and room for the camels.” His words are warm and his welcome generous. He uses the covenant name of God, YHWH, calling the servant “blessed of the LORD.” Rebekah must have told him how the stranger had prayed and praised the LORD God of Abraham, and Laban picks up the language.

The phrase shows that the LORD’s name was known in Nahor’s family. Terah’s household had worshipped other gods in Mesopotamia (Joshua 24:2), yet some knowledge of the true God survived among Abraham’s relatives, perhaps preserved by family tradition and by reports of Abraham’s prosperity in Canaan. Laban will later speak of the LORD again (v. 50; 30:27; 31:49), while also keeping household gods (31:30). His religion was a mixture: he acknowledged the LORD without giving him undivided loyalty.

That combination is a warning. It is possible to use God’s name correctly, even to speak of his blessing, while one’s heart remains attached to other things. Jesus said, “Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father” (Matthew 7:21). Laban’s greeting is sincere enough as courtesy, but his later conduct shows that his first loyalty was to his own interests.

Still, God uses Laban’s hospitality. The servant needed a home in which to tell his story, and Laban provides it. “I have prepared the house” uses a verb meaning “to clear” or “make room”; Laban has set things in order for the guests and their animals. Providence works even through people whose motives are mixed, as it will later work through Laban’s household to give Jacob his wives and children.

wordNotes.term: בְּרוּךְ יְהוָה (berukh YHWH) — blessed of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: A passive participle with the divine name: one who has received the LORD’s blessing. Abimelech uses the same phrase of Isaac in 26:29. On Laban’s lips it acknowledges the evident prosperity of Abraham’s household, though his later words show it did not reflect wholehearted faith.

The verb panah, “to turn,” in this intensive form means to clear away or make ready, as in preparing a road or a house. Isaiah uses it for preparing the way of the LORD, an image John the Baptist applied to his own ministry.

verses.bibleText: And the man came into the house: and he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet, and the men's feet that were with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the man came into the house: and he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet, and the men’s feet that were with him.” The servant accepts the invitation. The camels are unloaded and fed, and water is brought for washing. This is the first mention that the servant did not travel alone; men accompanied him, presumably to handle the caravan and protect its goods.

The Hebrew allows that Laban was the one who unloaded and fed the camels, or that the servant did so himself while water was brought by the household. Either way, the hospitality is complete. Washing travellers’ feet was a basic courtesy in a land of dusty roads and open sandals. Abraham had offered water for his guests’ feet (18:4), and Lot did the same (19:2). Jesus later noted that Simon the Pharisee had neglected this courtesy (Luke 7:44), and he himself washed his disciples’ feet as a lesson in humble service (John 13:5).

The narrator lingers on these details of welcome to slow the story before the servant’s speech. Everything is ready for a meal, for rest, and for conversation. The tension that remains is whether the servant will be able to say what he came to say.

The servant’s companions appear only now, washed and fed alongside him. They had shared the long road and the waiting at the well. The household’s care for them shows that hospitality extended to the whole party, not just to its leader. In the same spirit, Abraham had fed and refreshed every member of his visitors’ company at Mamre.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means “to loosen” or “open,” here used of untying the loads and harness from the camels. The same verb describes loosening a captive’s bonds in Psalm 116:16 and Isaiah 58:6.

verses.bibleText: And there was set meat before him to eat: but he said, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. And he said, Speak on.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Food is set before the servant, but he refuses to eat: “I will not eat, until I have told mine errand.” Ancient custom required hosts to feed guests before discussing business, and to decline a meal could seem discourteous. The servant takes that risk because his mission comes first. He will not relax at table while the purpose of his journey remains unsettled.

Several motives may lie behind his refusal. He is a man under oath, and he feels its weight. He wants to state his business openly so that no one can say he accepted hospitality under false pretences. Eating together in that culture created a bond of friendship and obligation; by speaking first, he ensures that any agreement reached will rest on a full understanding of his errand. He may also sense the need for caution with Laban, whose eagerness was sparked by gold.

Laban’s reply is brief: “Speak on.” The way is open for the servant’s long speech, the centre of the chapter.

The servant’s priority recalls Jesus at Sychar. When his disciples urged him to eat, he answered, “My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work” (John 4:34). Both men put the errand entrusted to them above their own comfort. The servant had travelled for weeks, watered at the well, and walked into a strange house, yet he would not eat until his master’s business was done.

There is a lesson here for anyone entrusted with God’s work. Faithfulness means attending first to what we were sent to do, before turning to our own needs. The servant’s example is not harsh self-denial but a clear sense of priority. Once his errand is accomplished, he will eat and drink gladly (v. 54).

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “my words” or “my matters.” Davar can mean both a spoken word and the matter or business a word concerns. The servant has a message to deliver and a matter to settle. The same word returns in verse 50, “the thing proceedeth from the LORD.”

An imperative of the verb “to speak,” giving permission to proceed. In context it is a host’s courteous consent to hear his guest’s business before the meal, departing from the normal order out of respect for the guest’s wishes.

verses.bibleText: And he said, I am Abraham's servant.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant begins with four Hebrew words: “I am Abraham’s servant.” He does not give his own name, and the narrator never supplies it. His whole identity is bound up with the man he serves. Leading with Abraham’s name also tells the family at once that this is a matter of kinship; Abraham was Nahor’s brother, and news of him would have reached the household.

His self-effacement is fitting for a messenger. A faithful envoy points away from himself to the one who sent him, as John the Baptist did when he said of Christ, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

wordNotes.explanation: ‘Eved can mean slave, servant, or official, depending on context. Here it marks a trusted steward who acts for his lord. The title “servant of the LORD” is later given to Moses and to the messianic Servant of Isaiah.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD hath blessed my master greatly; and he is become great: and he hath given him flocks, and herds, and silver, and gold, and menservants, and maidservants, and camels, and asses.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant’s first point is that “the LORD hath blessed my master greatly; and he is become great.” He then lists the evidence: flocks and herds, silver and gold, menservants and maidservants, camels and asses. The list resembles the narrator’s earlier notes on Abraham’s wealth (12:16; 13:2), but the servant credits every item to the LORD. He presents Abraham’s prosperity as a testimony to God’s favour, not as a boast.

The point is persuasive as well as theological. A family considering sending a daughter far away would want to know she was going to a secure household. The camels in their courtyard already proved the claim. Yet the servant’s emphasis is that the LORD has done this, preparing the family to see the hand of the same God in what happened at the well. The narrator’s statement in verse 1 now becomes the servant’s testimony.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּגְדָּל (vayyigdal) — and he is become great
wordNotes.explanation: The verb gadal means to grow or become great. It recalls God’s promise “I will make thy name great” (12:2). Isaac too will become “very great” through the LORD’s blessing.

verses.bibleText: And Sarah my master's wife bare a son to my master when she was old: and unto him hath he given all that he hath.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Next the servant introduces the bridegroom: “Sarah my master’s wife bare a son to my master when she was old: and unto him hath he given all that he hath.” Two facts matter. First, the son was born when Sarah was old. That points to the miracle of Isaac’s birth (18:11–14; 21:1–2), though the servant does not dwell on it, and it also explains why a son of so aged a father is still young enough to marry. Second, Isaac is the sole heir. Abraham has given him everything, as 25:5 confirms. Whoever marries Isaac will become mistress of the entire estate.

Strikingly, the servant never names Isaac in his speech. He is always “my master’s son.” The focus remains on Abraham and on the LORD’s blessing, with Isaac presented as its heir. Sarah, however, is named. As the mother of the bridegroom, her place matters to a family weighing a marriage, and her death leaves a place Rebekah will fill (v. 67).

wordNotes.term: אַחֲרֵי זִקְנָתָהּ (’acharei ziqnatah) — when she was old
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “after her old age,” that is, after she had passed the normal years of childbearing. The same root describes Abraham’s age in verse 1 and Sarah’s in 18:11–13. Paul and Hebrews point to this as evidence that Isaac’s birth was God’s gift received by faith.

verses.bibleText: And my master made me swear, saying, Thou shalt not take a wife to my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant reports the oath, slightly reshaped.
