He omits the gesture of the hand under the thigh and the full divine title of verse 3, and he says “in whose land I dwell” rather than “among whom I dwell.” The change makes Abraham’s refusal of Canaanite wives sound less like a judgment on neighbours and more like a statement of his situation: he lives in a land belonging to others, and he wants his son’s wife to come from his own people.

The effect on the listeners is a compliment. Abraham has passed over all the women of Canaan in order to seek a wife from Nahor’s house. The servant tells the truth, but he tells it in a way that honours his hearers.

wordNotes.explanation: “In his land,” referring to the Canaanite as owner of the land in which Abraham lives as a sojourner. The phrase fits Abraham’s self-description as “a stranger and a sojourner” in 23:4.

verses.bibleText: But thou shalt go unto my father's house, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
In verse 4 Abraham had said, “my country, and … my kindred.” The servant now says, “my father’s house, and … my kindred,” using a word for clan or family. The emphasis shifts from the region to the household. Abraham’s concern, as the servant presents it, was for this very family, the house of his father Terah to which Nahor belonged. The wording draws Rebekah’s family closer to Abraham and quietly prepares them to see her as the obvious choice.

The servant also avoids any reference to Abraham having left that country at God’s command. He does not reopen old wounds or suggest that Abraham judged them. Wise speech chooses what to emphasise without distorting the facts.

wordNotes.explanation: Mishpachah refers to a clan or extended family, a smaller unit than a tribe. It is the word used in 12:3, “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed,” linking Abraham’s family to God’s purpose for every clan.

verses.bibleText: And I said unto my master, Peradventure the woman will not follow me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant repeats his question to Abraham, “Peradventure the woman will not follow me,” but leaves out his suggestion that Isaac might go back to Mesopotamia (v. 5). He also leaves out Abraham’s firm refusal. To tell Nahor’s family that Abraham would not let his son set foot in their country would hardly help his cause.

The omission is tactful, and it keeps the focus where he wants it: on whether the woman will come. Nothing he says is false; he simply leaves unsaid what would wound his hearers without serving the purpose of his visit.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “will not go,” using halakh, the key verb of the chapter. The question of whether the woman will go returns in verses 55–58, where Rebekah answers with the same verb.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto me, The LORD, before whom I walk, will send his angel with thee, and prosper thy way; and thou shalt take a wife for my son of my kindred, and of my father's house:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant now quotes Abraham’s answer, again with changes. Abraham had spoken of the LORD who took him from his father’s house and swore to give his seed the land (v. 7). The servant replaces this with a new description: “The LORD, before whom I walk.” The phrase recalls God’s command to Abraham in 17:1, “walk before me, and be thou perfect.” Instead of stressing Abraham’s departure from the family, which his listeners might resent, the servant presents him as a man who lives in God’s presence and under his care.

He also expands the promise. Abraham said God would send his angel “before thee”; the servant says “with thee,” and adds “and prosper thy way.” That word, “prosper,” is the one he used at the well (v. 21) and will use again (vv. 42, 56). He is building his case that the success of his journey is the LORD’s doing, promised in advance.

The land promise is omitted entirely. To speak of Canaan as God’s gift to Abraham’s descendants was not necessary for this audience, and the servant keeps to what will help them decide.

wordNotes.term: הִתְהַלַּכְתִּי לְפָנָיו (hithallakhti lefanav) — before whom I walk
wordNotes.explanation: The reflexive form of halakh means to walk about, to conduct one’s life. To walk “before” God is to live consciously in his sight and service. Jacob uses the phrase of Abraham and Isaac on his deathbed, and Hezekiah pleads that he has walked before God in truth.

verses.bibleText: Then shalt thou be clear from this my oath, when thou comest to my kindred; and if they give not thee one, thou shalt be clear from my oath.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The release clause has also shifted. Abraham said the servant would be clear if the woman was unwilling (v. 8). The servant reports two conditions: he is clear “when thou comest to my kindred,” and “if they give not thee one.” The decision now seems to rest with the family rather than with the woman. The servant has transferred responsibility to his hearers. If they refuse, he is free; but they will bear the responsibility for frustrating what God has evidently arranged.

He also uses a stronger word for oath, one that includes the idea of a curse invoked on the oath-breaker. The family is reminded that a sacred obligation hangs over the matter.

wordNotes.explanation: ’Alah is an oath reinforced by a curse on anyone who breaks it. Verse 8 used shevu‘ah, the ordinary word for oath. The covenant with Abimelech in 26:28 and the covenant in Moab are both called an ’alah.

verses.bibleText: And I came this day unto the well, and said, O LORD God of my master Abraham, if now thou do prosper my way which I go:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And I came this day unto the well.” The servant moves from Abraham’s house to the scene just hours earlier. The words “this day” bring his hearers into the immediate past; everything he is about to describe happened that same evening, at their own well, involving their own daughter.

His prayer is recast slightly: “if now thou do prosper my way which I go.” At the well he asked God to “send me good speed” and “shew kindness unto my master” (v. 12). Now he speaks of God prospering his way, linking his prayer to the promise he has just quoted from Abraham (v. 40). The whole speech is unified by this theme: the LORD promised success, the servant asked for it, and God gave it.

wordNotes.explanation: The participle of the causative verb: “if you are prospering.” The servant asks God to make his journey reach its goal. The word becomes the refrain of the speech and of his plea to leave in verse 56.

verses.bibleText: Behold, I stand by the well of water; and it shall come to pass, that when the virgin cometh forth to draw water, and I say to her, Give me, I pray thee, a little water of thy pitcher to drink;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant repeats his description of standing by the well, but one word changes. In verse 14 he prayed about “the damsel” (na‘arah); now he speaks of “the virgin” (‘almah), a term for a young woman of marriageable age who is not yet married. The change suits his audience; he is speaking to her family about a prospective bride.

This is one of the few places where ‘almah occurs, and it is the word Isaiah uses in the sign of Immanuel: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14). Rebekah is both ‘almah here and betulah in verse 16, showing that an ‘almah in the ordinary course of life was expected to be a virgin. The Greek translators of Genesis rendered ‘almah here with parthenos, the same word used in Isaiah 7:14 and quoted in Matthew 1:23 of Mary. The usage in Genesis 24 thus supports the sense that Matthew draws from Isaiah.

wordNotes.explanation: ‘Almah denotes a young woman of marriageable age who has not yet married. It describes Miriam as a girl watching over Moses and the maidens of Song of Solomon 6:8. In Genesis 24 the same young woman is called ‘almah and betulah, and the Greek version renders ‘almah here as parthenos, “virgin,” as it does in Isaiah 7:14.

verses.bibleText: And she say to me, Both drink thou, and I will also draw for thy camels: let the same be the woman whom the LORD hath appointed out for my master's son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The terms of the sign are restated, now shortened: “Both drink thou, and I will also draw for thy camels.” Then the servant names the conclusion he drew: “let the same be the woman whom the LORD hath appointed out for my master’s son.”

At the well he spoke to God directly, “thou hast appointed for thy servant Isaac” (v. 14). Speaking to the family, he refers to the LORD in the third person and to Isaac as “my master’s son,” but the claim is the same: God has already chosen.

wordNotes.term: הֹכִיחַ יְהוָה (hokhiach YHWH) — the LORD hath appointed
wordNotes.explanation: The same verb as in verse 14, now with the divine name stated. Proverbs says that while houses and riches come from parents, “a prudent wife is from the LORD,” a fitting summary of the servant’s conviction.

verses.bibleText: And before I had done speaking in mine heart, behold, Rebekah came forth with her pitcher on her shoulder; and she went down unto the well, and drew water: and I said unto her, Let me drink, I pray thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant now reveals something the narrator left implicit: “before I had done speaking in mine heart.” His prayer at the well was silent. No one could have overheard it, and Rebekah could not have known what he was asking. Her offer to water the camels was therefore entirely her own. That detail matters for his argument. There was no collusion or prompting; God answered a prayer spoken only in the heart.

Otherwise the account of her arrival is condensed. The description of her beauty and virginity (v. 16) is omitted; her family hardly needs it. The narrative moves straight to the request for water. Hannah’s prayer in the temple was also spoken in her heart, with only her lips moving (1 Samuel 1:13), and God heard her too.

wordNotes.term: לְדַבֵּר אֶל־לִבִּי (ledabber ’el-libbi) — speaking in mine heart
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “speaking to my heart,” an idiom for silent thought or inward speech. Hannah prayed in the same way, and the fool “hath said in his heart” in the Psalms. Here it means the prayer was unspoken aloud.

verses.bibleText: And she made haste, and let down her pitcher from her shoulder, and said, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: so I drank, and she made the camels drink also.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah’s response is summarised in a single sentence. “She made haste … and said, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: so I drank, and she made the camels drink also.” The account omits the long labour of verse 20, the running back and forth to the spring.

Her family already knew how much she had done that evening. The servant simply confirms that she said and did exactly what his silent prayer had specified. The repetition of “drink” and “also” echoes the wording of the sign, so that the match between request and answer is heard as well as told.

wordNotes.explanation: The causative form of shaqah, “to drink”: she gave drink to the camels. It is the same verb used for watering flocks in the stories of Jacob and Moses at wells.

verses.bibleText: And I asked her, and said, Whose daughter art thou? And she said, The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bare unto him: and I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here the most noticeable change occurs. In the narrative the servant gave the gold before asking Rebekah’s family (vv. 22–23). In his retelling he asks first, “Whose daughter art thou?” and only then says, “I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands.” The order he gives is the one that would reassure her family: he did not adorn a stranger’s daughter until he knew she was their kin.

The difference may reflect a summary arranged by logic rather than by sequence, or it may show the servant presenting his actions in their most proper light. He does not invent anything; the gifts were given and the question was asked. Biblical narrative often allows characters to tell the same events with different emphases, and the reader is expected to notice.

He also reports Rebekah’s answer in a slightly different form, naming Bethuel as Nahor’s son and Milcah as his mother. The genealogy is now told in the order most natural for the family listening.

wordNotes.term: וָאָשִׂם הַנֶּזֶם עַל־אַפָּהּ (va’asim hannezem ‘al-’appah) — and I put the earring upon her face
wordNotes.explanation: ’Af means “nose” or “nostril,” hence also “face.” The phrase confirms that the nezem was a nose ring. Ezekiel uses the same imagery when the LORD describes adorning Jerusalem as his bride.

verses.bibleText: And I bowed down my head, and worshipped the LORD, and blessed the LORD God of my master Abraham, which had led me in the right way to take my master's brother's daughter unto his son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant ends his account with his worship: “I bowed down my head, and worshipped the LORD, and blessed the LORD God of my master Abraham, which had led me in the right way.” He wants the family to know that he did not take credit for the outcome. He gave thanks to God at the well, before he had even entered their home.

The phrase “the right way” translates “the way of truth.” In verse 27 he praised God’s mercy and truth; now he describes the road itself as a way of truth, a dependable path on which God led him. The way was reliable because the God who guided it was faithful.

He describes Rebekah as “my master’s brother’s daughter.” She was actually the granddaughter of Abraham’s brother. Hebrew uses “brother” and “daughter” broadly for relatives, and the point is clear: God led him to Abraham’s own family, exactly as Abraham had required. The goal was not merely a wife but a wife of the right lineage, “unto his son.”

wordNotes.term: בְּדֶרֶךְ אֱמֶת (bederekh ’emet) — in the right way
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “in a way of truth,” meaning a road that is sure and dependable. Emet links the path to God’s faithfulness praised in verse 27. The psalmist prays to be led in God’s truth and taught his paths.

verses.bibleText: And now if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me: and if not, tell me; that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having finished his story, the servant puts the question: “And now if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me: and if not, tell me; that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left.” He uses the same pair of words he used of God in verse 27, chesed and emet, kindness and truth. God has shown faithful love to Abraham; will Abraham’s kin do the same? The servant invites them to align their decision with what God has evidently done.

He does not pressure them with threats or bargaining. He asks for a clear answer, yes or no. If they refuse, he will “turn to the right hand, or to the left,” that is, look elsewhere. The phrase is vague, perhaps deliberately so, and it hints that he has no other plan. His confidence rests on God’s leading, not on alternatives.

The servant’s request models honest dealing. He has told his whole errand before eating their food, and he asks for a direct reply before going further. Jesus taught, “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Matthew 5:37). The servant wants the same plainness from his hosts. The decision now lies with them, but the reader already knows that God has prepared the way.

His words also show how human faithfulness can mirror God’s. Chesed and emet describe God’s covenant loyalty, but they are also qualities God expects of his people in their dealings with one another (Proverbs 3:3; Hosea 4:1). Rebekah’s family is invited to act toward Abraham as God has acted.

wordNotes.term: עֹשִׂים חֶסֶד וֶאֱמֶת (‘osim chesed ve’emet) — deal kindly and truly
wordNotes.explanation: “To do faithful love and truth” describes acting with loyal kindness that can be relied on. Jacob asks Joseph to deal with him in this way regarding his burial, and the spies promise it to Rahab. Here the family is asked to respond to God’s chesed with their own.

wordNotes.term: יָמִין אוֹ עַל־שְׂמֹאל (yamin ’o ‘al-semo’l) — the right hand, or … the left
wordNotes.explanation: An idiom for turning in another direction. Elsewhere Scripture uses it of not swerving from God’s law, but here it simply means the servant will seek another course if refused.

verses.bibleText: Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, The thing proceedeth from the LORD: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, The thing proceedeth from the LORD: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good.” The family’s answer is a confession that God has decided the matter. The servant’s account has convinced them. The meeting at the well, the sign fulfilled by Rebekah’s own unprompted kindness, the family connection, and the evident blessing on Abraham’s house all point in one direction. They recognise that to oppose the marriage would be to oppose the LORD.

The order of names is unusual. Laban, the son, is named before Bethuel, the father. Elsewhere in the story Bethuel is absent, and the mother and brother take the leading part (vv. 28, 53, 55). It seems likely that Bethuel was aged or infirm and that Laban acted as head of the household in practice, but the father’s name is included because a marriage required his consent.

“We cannot speak unto thee bad or good” is an idiom meaning they have nothing to add; the decision is not theirs to make. They neither oppose nor negotiate. The same expression appears when God warns Laban in a dream years later not to speak to Jacob “either good or bad” (31:24, 29). In both cases God’s will overrides Laban’s own wishes. Here he yields readily; later he will yield under compulsion.

The confession is remarkable coming from a household that also served other gods. The evidence of providence was plain enough that even Laban, whose eyes were on the gold, acknowledged the LORD’s hand. God’s works can bear witness to people who do not yet know him well. When Peter recounted how God had given the Spirit to Gentiles, the believers in Jerusalem “held their peace, and glorified God” (Acts 11:17–18), recognising that they could not withstand what God had done. Rebekah’s family reaches a similar conclusion about this marriage.

wordNotes.term: מֵיְהוָה יָצָא הַדָּבָר (meYHWH yatsa’ haddavar) — the thing proceedeth from the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: “The matter has gone out from the LORD,” that is, he has decided it. Davar here means the affair or matter, not merely a spoken word. Similar language is used when God sends a word that will not return empty and when Rehoboam’s division of the kingdom is said to be “from the LORD.”

A merism using two opposites to mean “anything at all.” The family has nothing to say for or against. The phrase recurs when God forbids Laban to speak to Jacob “either good or bad,” and when Absalom says nothing to Amnon “neither good nor bad.”

verses.bibleText: Behold, Rebekah is before thee, take her, and go, and let her be thy master's son's wife, as the LORD hath spoken.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The family gives its formal consent: “Behold, Rebekah is before thee, take her, and go, and let her be thy master’s son’s wife, as the LORD hath spoken.” They place Rebekah, so to speak, in the servant’s hands. The words “take her, and go” are the language of agreement, releasing her to the household of Abraham. Ironically, Pharaoh had used almost the same words when returning Sarah to Abraham: “behold thy wife, take her, and go thy way” (12:19). There the words ended a crisis Abraham had brought upon himself; here they bring God’s plan to its next step.

“As the LORD hath spoken” is striking. God has not spoken aloud in this chapter. No vision, voice, or angel has appeared. Yet the family understands that God has made his will known through the events at the well. Providence can speak as clearly as words when people pay attention to it. The servant’s faithful account of what happened has allowed them to hear what God was saying.

The consent is given before Rebekah is formally asked. In that culture the family’s agreement to a marriage was the normal first step. But the story will not leave the matter there. When the question of timing arises, Rebekah herself will be asked and will answer (vv. 57–58). Her family’s consent and her own will both be part of the outcome.

The servant’s mission is now, in principle, accomplished. A wife has been found from Abraham’s kindred, and her family has agreed to let her go to Canaan. Everything Abraham asked for has been granted, and the release clause of the oath (v. 8) will not be needed.

wordNotes.term: קַח וָלֵךְ (qach valekh) — take her, and go
wordNotes.explanation: Two imperatives that formally release Rebekah to Abraham’s household. The same pair of verbs appears in Pharaoh’s words in 12:19. They also echo the two verbs Abraham used in commissioning the servant: “go … and take a wife” (v. 4).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, that, when Abraham's servant heard their words, he worshipped the LORD, bowing himself to the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass, that, when Abraham’s servant heard their words, he worshipped the LORD, bowing himself to the earth.” For the third time in the chapter the servant turns to God (vv. 12, 26). At the well he bowed his head; now he bows himself to the ground. His worship deepens as the answer becomes complete.

He worships before he thanks the family, before he brings out the gifts, and before he eats. The servant never treats the outcome as his own achievement. Whatever skill he showed in telling his story, he knows the decisive work was God’s. His response teaches that every step of God’s guidance calls for gratitude, not only the final result.

His worship also bears witness in Laban’s house. A household that mixed the LORD’s name with household gods sees a man bow to the ground before the one God of Abraham. He does not lecture them; he simply worships. The habits of a faithful servant can testify to God where words might not be welcome. Paul urged believers to give thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and the servant’s life is a pattern of that practice: prayer at the start, thanks at each answer, and humble acknowledgement that the LORD has done it.

Bowing to the earth was the posture Abraham had used before his heavenly visitors at Mamre (18:2). The servant has learned not only his master’s faith but his master’s manner of worship.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ אַרְצָה (vayyishtachu ’artsah) — bowing himself to the earth
wordNotes.explanation: The verb of prostration with “to the ground” describes the fullest posture of homage. Abraham bowed this way to his visitors at Mamre, and Moses bowed to the earth when the LORD proclaimed his name.

verses.bibleText: And the servant brought forth jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave them to Rebekah: he gave also to her brother and to her mother precious things.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With the agreement settled, the servant opens his treasures: “the servant brought forth jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave them to Rebekah: he gave also to her brother and to her mother precious things.” The gifts to Rebekah are her own, a rich wardrobe and jewellery suited to the bride of a wealthy household. The gifts to her brother and mother are probably the bride-price or marriage gift, a customary payment to the bride’s family that sealed the betrothal and compensated them for her departure (34:12; Exodus 22:16–17).

The generosity matches the wealth the servant described (v. 35). It also shows that the household of promise is able to care for her. Rebekah’s family had been told of Abraham’s blessing; now they see it in their hands.

The mention of the mother is notable. Bethuel is again passed over, and the gifts go to Laban and his mother. Whatever Bethuel’s condition, the mother and brother are the active figures in the household’s dealings.

The scene recalls the language Scripture later uses for God’s relationship with his people. In Ezekiel 16 the LORD describes clothing his bride in embroidered garments and adorning her with jewels. In Revelation the bride of the Lamb is “arrayed in fine linen, clean and white” (Revelation 19:8). The gifts of a bridegroom’s house are signs of love and of the life to which the bride is called. Rebekah, clothed and adorned by Abraham’s servant, is being prepared to enter the household of promise.

wordNotes.explanation: The word refers to choice or costly gifts. It describes the gifts neighbours gave the returning exiles, the treasures Jehoshaphat left his sons, and the presents brought to Hezekiah. The gifts were a token of honour and binding agreement.

wordNotes.term: כְּלֵי־כֶסֶף וּכְלֵי זָהָב (kelei-khesef ukhlei zahav) — jewels of silver, and jewels of gold
wordNotes.explanation: Keli is a general word for an article or object, here referring to ornaments and vessels of precious metal. Israel later asked the Egyptians for such “jewels of silver, and jewels of gold” before the exodus.

verses.bibleText: And they did eat and drink, he and the men that were with him, and tarried all night; and they rose up in the morning, and he said, Send me away unto my master.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Only now does the servant eat: “they did eat and drink, he and the men that were with him, and tarried all night.” With his errand fulfilled, he can rest. The meal he refused in verse 33 is now accepted. Eating together seals the agreement between the two households. Covenant meals appear elsewhere in Genesis, as when Isaac feasted with Abimelech (26:30) and Jacob with Laban (31:54).

The next morning the servant is ready to leave: “Send me away unto my master.” He does not linger. Abraham is old, and the servant knows his master is waiting for news. His sense of duty, so evident in his refusal to eat before speaking, now shows itself in his eagerness to return. The task is not complete until the bride has been brought home.

The brief verse shows a balanced faithfulness. The servant was not ascetic; he enjoyed the meal once the time was right. Nor was he indifferent to his hosts; he spent the night as their guest. But he never lost sight of his commission. A faithful servant enjoys the gifts of the way without forgetting where he is going. Jesus’ parable of the faithful steward commends the one his master finds doing his duty when he returns (Luke 12:42–43). Abraham’s servant shows the same diligence.

His urgency also reflects his oath. The servant had sworn to take a wife for Isaac and bring her back. Until Rebekah reached Canaan, his obligation was not yet discharged. A faithful servant measures success not by a promising start but by completing the task he was given.

wordNotes.explanation: The intensive form of shalach, “to send,” means to send off or dismiss, often with farewell and blessing. Jacob uses it when asking Laban to let him return home, and Moses’ repeated demand to Pharaoh, “Let my people go,” uses the same verb.

verses.bibleText: And her brother and her mother said, Let the damsel abide with us a few days, at the least ten; after that she shall go.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah’s brother and mother ask for delay: “Let the damsel abide with us a few days, at the least ten; after that she shall go.” Their request is natural. A daughter was leaving home for a distant country, probably never to return. They wanted time to prepare her, to say farewell, and perhaps to hold a feast. Their affection is real, and the request is not unreasonable by the customs of the time.

The Hebrew is unusual, literally “days or ten.” It could mean “a few days, say ten,” as the KJV renders it. Some ancient interpreters understood “days” in the sense of a year and read “a year or ten months.” The vagueness may itself be telling. A request for “days” could stretch indefinitely. Years later, Laban would keep Jacob for twenty years, repeatedly finding reasons to extend his stay (31:41).

Once again the brother and mother act together, with Bethuel absent. The narrator gives no explicit criticism, but the reader has learned to watch Laban. The family had agreed the night before that Rebekah could “take … and go” (v. 51); now they hesitate. Second thoughts after a firm agreement are a familiar human weakness, but they can also become a way of quietly undoing what God has arranged.

The tension of the story returns. Everything seemed settled, but a new obstacle appears. Will the servant be held back? The question of Rebekah’s willingness, raised in verse 5, will come to the fore again.

wordNotes.term: יָמִים אוֹ עָשׂוֹר (yamim ’o ‘asor) — a few days, at the least ten
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “days or ten.” The phrase is ambiguous. “Days” sometimes means a year (Leviticus 25:29), and ancient Jewish interpretation read it as “a year or ten months.” The Greek version took it as “about ten days.” Either way, the family sought to postpone the departure.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto them, Hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The servant refuses: “Hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master.” His argument is theological. The LORD has prospered his journey; delaying its completion would mean holding back what God has evidently blessed. He frames the request not as personal impatience but as obedience to providence.

The servant had good reason for urgency. Abraham was very old, and news of the mission’s success should reach him as soon as possible. A long stay might also give the family time to change its mind or bargain further. The servant had seen Laban’s interest in gold, and he may have sensed that delay would bring complications. Time is not neutral when God has opened a door. Opportunities can be lost through hesitation.

The word “prospered” returns for the last time. The servant has asked for it (v. 42), watched for it (v. 21), reported it as promised (v. 40), and now claims it as accomplished. His entire mission rests on the conviction that God, not he, has made the journey successful.

The principle of prompt obedience appears often in Scripture. Abraham rose early to obey God’s command (22:3). The psalmist says, “I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments” (Psalm 119:60). When God makes his will clear, delay can be a form of disobedience. The servant’s firmness serves both his master and the purpose of God, and it brings the question of Rebekah’s will to the fore.

wordNotes.explanation: The intensive form of ’achar, “to be behind,” means to delay or hold back. Moses uses the same verb when commanding Israel not to be slow in paying vows, and the psalmist uses a related form in begging God not to tarry.

verses.bibleText: And they said, We will call the damsel, and enquire at her mouth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The family responds, “We will call the damsel, and enquire at her mouth.” Faced with the servant’s insistence, they turn the decision over to Rebekah. Her consent to the marriage itself has been assumed; what is now asked is whether she will go immediately.

Their motive may be mixed. They may hope that Rebekah, given the choice, will prefer to stay a while longer at home. A young woman facing a long journey to marry a stranger might well want time. If so, their appeal to her would gain the delay they want without their having to refuse the servant directly.

Whatever their reasons, the result is to give Rebekah a voice. The story has been building toward this moment since the servant first asked, “Peradventure the woman will not be willing” (v. 5). Abraham insisted that the woman must be willing (v. 8). Now her willingness will be tested. In the ancient world a daughter’s marriage was usually arranged by her family, yet her consent was not ignored, and here it becomes decisive.

God’s purposes for Rebekah do not bypass her own will. She has been chosen and prepared, and her family has consented; but the step of going must be hers. God’s calling is never mere compulsion. It invites a response.

The family’s question to Rebekah also confirms what Abraham had foreseen. He had said the woman must be willing to follow (v. 8). The narrator now shows that God’s plan, though prepared by many hands, rests finally on a free and personal decision. No one could make it for her.

wordNotes.term: וְנִשְׁאֲלָה אֶת־פִּיהָ (venish’alah ’et-piha) — and enquire at her mouth
wordNotes.explanation: “Let us ask her mouth,” an idiom for consulting someone directly and hearing their own answer. The same idiom is used, negatively, of Israel failing to ask counsel at the LORD’s mouth. Here it gives Rebekah the right to speak for herself.

verses.bibleText: And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.” In Hebrew her answer is a single word, ’elekh, “I will go.” It is the decisive moment of the chapter. Everything else has been prepared: the oath, the journey, the prayer, the sign, the family’s consent, the gifts. Now the outcome depends on the free choice of a young woman, and she chooses without hesitation.

The question is put plainly. “With this man” refers to the servant, a stranger she met the previous evening. To go with him meant leaving her mother, her brother, and her home, travelling hundreds of miles to a land she had never seen, and marrying a man she knew only by report. She would probably never see her family again. Yet she does not ask for time or conditions.

Her “I will go” echoes Abraham’s own departure. When God called Abraham out of the same region, Genesis records simply, “So Abram departed” (12:4), using the same verb. Rebekah steps into the same path of faith. She leaves country, kindred, and father’s house to go to the land of promise, joining the family through whom all nations would be blessed. Hebrews describes Abraham as going out “not knowing whither he went” (Hebrews 11:8). Rebekah knew little more. She went on the strength of what she had heard and seen of the LORD’s leading.

Her decision recalls another young woman who left her homeland for the God of Israel. Ruth said to Naomi, “whither thou goest, I will go” (Ruth 1:16), and she too became an ancestor of the messianic line. Both women’s choices were moments of faith on which God’s purposes turned.

The story invites every reader to consider the same question. God calls people to leave the old life and follow him toward an inheritance not yet seen. The call comes through messengers who tell what God has done, and it asks for a response. Jesus called his disciples with the words “Follow me,” and they “left all, and followed him” (Luke 5:27–28). Rebekah’s answer is the answer of faith in every generation: “I will go.”

wordNotes.explanation: The first person imperfect of halakh, the key verb of the chapter. Rebekah’s one-word reply answers the question raised since verse 5 and echoes Abraham’s obedient going in 12:4. Ruth uses the same verb in her pledge to Naomi, and Isaiah answers God’s call with the related “Here am I; send me.”

verses.bibleText: And they sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham's servant, and his men.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah’s decision settles the matter: “they sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham’s servant, and his men.” The family accepts her choice and releases her. The verb “sent away” is the one the servant used when asking to be dismissed (vv. 54, 56). His request is now granted.

Rebekah does not go alone. Her nurse accompanies her. In the ancient world a nurse who had cared for a girl from infancy often remained with her as companion, guardian, and adviser into adulthood. Genesis later gives this nurse’s name, Deborah, and records her death and burial near Bethel, where she was mourned so deeply that the tree beneath which she was buried was named “the oak of weeping” (35:8). She must have served Rebekah’s household for decades, and her presence on the journey would have been a great comfort to a young woman leaving everything familiar.

Rebekah is called “their sister.” Laban was her brother, but the plural suggests the whole family regarded her as their sister in a wider sense, or it may reflect the brother’s prominence in sending her off. The word prepares for the blessing that follows, which begins, “Thou art our sister” (v. 60).

The departure is orderly and affectionate. The family that tried to delay her now sends her away with honour. Whatever the motives behind the request for delay, the parting is not hostile. Rebekah leaves with her family’s consent, her nurse beside her, and, as the next verse shows, their blessing upon her.

The household of promise is enlarged not only by a bride but by those who come with her. Deborah and Rebekah’s maids (v. 61) become part of the family of Abraham. God’s blessing often draws others in through the one he calls.

wordNotes.explanation: From yanaq, “to suckle,” the word refers to a wet nurse who fed a child in infancy and often remained as guardian and companion. Deborah, named in 35:8, is the nurse who went with Rebekah. Joash’s nurse hid him from Athaliah, showing the trust placed in such women.

verses.bibleText: And they blessed Rebekah, and said unto her, Thou art our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Before Rebekah leaves, her family pronounces a blessing: “Thou art our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them.” The words take a poetic form, two lines in parallel, as farewell blessings often did in the ancient world. They wish for her the two things a family most desired for a departing daughter: many descendants, and security and victory for them.

“Thousands of millions” translates “thousands of ten thousands,” the highest numbers in ordinary Hebrew use. The family hopes she will become the mother of a vast people. They do not know that God has already promised exactly that to Abraham’s seed, “as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore” (22:17). Their wish echoes the divine promise.

The second line is even closer. “Let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them” repeats almost word for word what the LORD swore to Abraham on Moriah: “thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies” (22:17). The gate of a city was the place of defence and government; to possess it was to control the city. Without knowing it, Rebekah’s family blesses her in the very terms of God’s covenant oath. The God who had promised the seed to Abraham now has the promise spoken over the woman who will carry it forward.

The blessing makes Rebekah a participant in the covenant promise. Sarah had been included in the promise to Abraham (17:16), and now Rebekah is too. The line of promise is carried not only through fathers but through mothers chosen by God. Through her son Jacob would come the twelve tribes, and through them, in the fullness of time, the Seed in whom all nations are blessed (Galatians 3:16).

The ultimate fulfilment of possessing the enemy’s gate is found in Christ’s victory. Jesus told Peter that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against” his church (Matthew 16:18). The Seed of the woman, promised in Eden (3:15), triumphs over every power that opposes God’s people. The family in Nahor’s city could not have understood how far their blessing would reach.

wordNotes.term: לְאַלְפֵי רְבָבָה (le’alfei revavah) — of thousands of millions
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “thousands of ten thousands,” the largest number phrase in common Hebrew, meaning a countless multitude. Moses uses a similar expression when the ark came to rest among Israel’s “many thousands,” and Daniel and Revelation use it of the hosts around God’s throne.

wordNotes.term: שַׁעַר שֹׂנְאָיו (sha‘ar sone’av) — the gate of those which hate them
wordNotes.explanation: The city gate was the seat of defence and judgment; to possess it meant to conquer the city. The phrase nearly repeats God’s oath to Abraham in 22:17, where the enemies are called “his enemies.” Here they are “those which hate him,” a synonym.

verses.bibleText: And Rebekah arose, and her damsels, and they rode upon the camels, and followed the man: and the servant took Rebekah, and went his way.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Rebekah arose, and her damsels, and they rode upon the camels, and followed the man: and the servant took Rebekah, and went his way.” Now it is clear why the servant brought ten camels. They carry Rebekah, her maids, and her nurse back to Canaan. The camels that knelt at the well on the evening of his arrival now carry the bride home.

Rebekah takes “her damsels,” young women who served her. Their presence shows that she came from a household of some standing. She does not arrive in Canaan as a poor dependent but as a woman with her own attendants, fit to take the place of the mistress of Abraham’s household.

The verbs in this verse summarise the story’s movement. Rebekah “arose” and “followed”; the servant “took” and “went.” These echo Abraham’s commission, “thou shalt go … and take a wife” (v. 4). The servant’s task, begun with an oath, is now nearly complete. He has gone, and he has taken. The narrator again passes over the long journey in silence, as with the journey north (v. 10). Weeks of travel are summed up in a phrase, “went his way.”

Rebekah follows a man she has known for a day toward a husband she has never seen. Her faith rests on the message she has heard and the evidence of God’s leading she has witnessed. Many Christians through the centuries have seen in this scene an illustration of the church, called through the message of God’s servant to leave the world and go to meet the Son whom she has not yet seen. Peter writes of Christ, “whom having not seen, ye love” (1 Peter 1:8). The text does not present itself as an allegory, and the comparison should not be pressed in every detail; but the pattern of a bride responding in faith to a bridegroom known only by report rings true to the gospel.

wordNotes.explanation: Young women who attended her, her maids. The same word describes the maidens who served Pharaoh’s daughter, Boaz’s gleaners, and Esther’s attendants. Their presence marks Rebekah’s social standing.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac came from the way of the well Lahai-roi; for he dwelt in the south country.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene shifts to Canaan and to Isaac, who has not appeared in person since the binding on Moriah. “And Isaac came from the way of the well Lahai-roi; for he dwelt in the south country.” Isaac is living in the Negeb, the dry southern region of Canaan, apparently apart from Abraham, who had been at Hebron when Sarah died (23:2). He has been near or returning from the well named by Hagar.

That well has a history. Hagar, fleeing from Sarah, met the Angel of the LORD there and called it Beer-lahai-roi, a name honouring the living God who had seen her (16:13–14). It was a place where God had shown himself as the One who sees and cares for the lonely and distressed. Isaac, still grieving his mother, is associated with that place. After Abraham’s death he will settle there (25:11).

The mention of a well is significant in another way. The servant met Rebekah at a well in Mesopotamia; Isaac now comes from a well in Canaan. The two well scenes frame the journey and suggest that the same God is at work at both ends. The God who sees at Lahai-roi has been watching over Isaac’s future while the servant travelled, and he has been arranging events far away for the good of a young man who did not know what was happening.

Isaac’s appearance here also marks a shift in the story. Abraham fades from view. He will not be mentioned again in this chapter, and the servant will report to Isaac instead (v. 66). The narrative is preparing the transition from one generation to the next. Isaac is becoming the head of the household of promise, and he will soon receive the wife God has chosen for him.

wordNotes.term: בְּאֵר לַחַי רֹאִי (Be’er Lachai Ro’i) — the well Lahai-roi
wordNotes.explanation: “The well of the Living One who sees me.” Hagar gave it this name after the Angel of the LORD found her in the wilderness. Isaac’s association with this place links him to the God who sees the afflicted, and he later dwells there.

The Negeb, the dry region south of the hill country of Judah, around Beersheba. Abraham journeyed there early (12:9) and lived there at times (20:1). The name comes from a root meaning “dry,” and it became the ordinary Hebrew word for “south.”

verses.bibleText: And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide: and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and, behold, the camels were coming.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide: and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and, behold, the camels were coming.” The time of day matches the servant’s arrival at the well (v. 11). Evening was the time of the servant’s prayer in Mesopotamia; it is now the time of Isaac’s meditation in Canaan. The two scenes mirror each other across the distance.

The word translated “meditate” is rare and its meaning uncertain. It occurs only here in this form. The oldest translations vary: the Greek has a word suggesting conversing or musing, the Latin Vulgate has “to meditate,” and the Aramaic Targum and Samaritan tradition read “to pray.” Some connect it with a similar verb used for complaint, lament, or pouring out one’s thoughts before God (Psalm 55:17 and the title of Psalm 102), which would fit a son still mourning his mother. Others relate it to a word meaning “to walk about” or “stroll.” The KJV’s “meditate” is a reasonable rendering that keeps the sense of reflective thought, possibly turned toward God in prayer.

Whatever the exact sense, Isaac is alone in the field at evening, thinking and perhaps praying. He may have been praying for the servant’s success or grieving the loss of Sarah, or both. His posture fits his character as Genesis portrays it: a quieter, more contemplative figure than his father or his son. He is not out working or travelling; he has gone out to be alone with his thoughts before God.

Then he looks up. The phrase “lifted up his eyes, and saw” is common in Genesis for a moment of discovery. Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place on Moriah, then saw the ram in the thicket (22:4, 13). Now Isaac lifts up his eyes and sees camels approaching. The very next verse will use the same expression for Rebekah. Their eyes meet across the field, each seeing the other at the same moment.

Isaac’s meditation at evening offers a quiet example. The psalmist speaks of meditating on God “in the night watches” (Psalm 63:6) and on his law “day and night” (Psalm 1:2). Time set apart for reflection and prayer is the setting in which many answers are first recognised. Isaac, waiting in the field, sees the answer coming over the horizon.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb occurs only here and its meaning is debated. Ancient versions render it as musing, meditating, or praying. A related verb siach is used for meditation, complaint, or pouring out one’s heart to God, as in Psalm 77, and fits Isaac’s grief. The KJV margin offers “to pray.” The context suggests reflective solitude before God.

Literally “at the turning of evening,” as the day declines. The servant arrived at the well at evening (v. 11), and Isaac goes out at the same hour. Evening was a customary time of prayer, and the evening sacrifice later marked it in Israel’s worship.

verses.bibleText: And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel.” The narrator uses the same phrase as in verse 63. Isaac lifted his eyes and saw the camels; Rebekah lifts her eyes and sees Isaac. The two glances happen together. After all the human planning and the long journey, the meeting of bride and groom is presented as a moment of mutual recognition.

She “lighted off the camel,” literally “fell from the camel,” an idiom for dismounting quickly. Getting down from a camel normally required the animal to kneel, and the expression suggests haste. Rebekah does not wait; she gets down at once. The gesture is one of respect, for in that culture a person of lower standing dismounted to greet a superior, as Achsah did before her father Caleb (Joshua 15:18) and Abigail before David (1 Samuel 25:23). She would not meet her future husband looking down at him from a camel’s height.

Her haste also fits her character throughout the story. She ran to water the camels, ran to tell her family, and answered “I will go” without delay. Now she quickly dismounts to meet the man walking toward them. Her eagerness is part of her readiness to embrace the life God has set before her.

The narrator does not say what she felt. The text lets actions speak: she sees, she dismounts, she asks who he is. The reader can sense curiosity, anticipation, and modesty all at once.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּפֹּל מֵעַל הַגָּמָל (vattippol me‘al haggamal) — she lighted off the camel
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “she fell from upon the camel,” an idiom for getting down quickly. Naaman likewise “lighted down from the chariot” (literally “fell”) to meet Gehazi. The phrase conveys both haste and respect.

verses.bibleText: For she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator explains Rebekah’s action: “she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself.” Rebekah asks the question any traveller might ask about a stranger approaching across a field. The servant’s answer is short: “It is my master.”

That answer marks a turning point. Throughout the chapter “my master” has meant Abraham. Now the servant uses it of Isaac. The transition of authority from father to son has taken place. Abraham will die soon (25:7–8), and the servant already recognises Isaac as the head of the household. Rebekah learns that the man walking toward her is not a stranger but the bridegroom she has travelled so far to meet.

Her response is to take a veil and cover herself. Women in that region did not usually wear veils in everyday life. Rebekah herself had been seen unveiled at the well, and Sarah’s beauty had been noticed in Egypt (12:14). The veil here was the sign of a bride. In ancient Near Eastern custom a bride was veiled before her husband until the marriage was completed, which is why Jacob could later be deceived into marrying Leah instead of Rachel (29:23–25). By veiling herself, Rebekah signals to Isaac that she is his bride, coming to him in modesty and reserve.

The act shows her respect for Isaac and her understanding of what this meeting means. She is not simply a traveller arriving at a new home; she is a bride presenting herself to her husband. Her modesty matches the honour with which she had greeted the servant at the well.

Scripture often uses the image of a bride prepared for her husband to describe God’s people. Revelation pictures the holy city as “a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2), and Paul speaks of presenting the church to Christ as a chaste virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2). Rebekah, veiled and ready, gives a human picture of the preparation and devotion with which the people of God await their Bridegroom.

wordNotes.explanation: A veil or wrap covering the face. The word occurs only in Genesis, here and in the story of Tamar, who used it to disguise herself. Rebekah’s veil marks her as Isaac’s bride, part of the custom by which the bride was veiled until the marriage.

wordNotes.term: הוּא אֲדֹנִי (hu’ ’adoni) — it is my master
wordNotes.explanation: Two words in Hebrew, with the pronoun “he” placed first for emphasis. For the first time the servant calls Isaac “my master,” a title used of Abraham throughout the chapter. The change marks the passing of headship to the son of promise.

verses.bibleText: And the servant told Isaac all things that he had done.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the servant told Isaac all things that he had done.” The servant reports to Isaac rather than to Abraham. The narrator does not mention any meeting with Abraham at all. Abraham sent the servant, but Isaac receives the report. The chapter, which opened with Abraham’s commission, closes with the son as head of the household.

The narrator also declines to repeat the story a second time. The servant’s detailed account to Rebekah’s family (vv. 34–49) has already shown how he would tell it. Here a single sentence suffices. “All things that he had done” would include the oath, the journey, the prayer at the well, the sign, the meeting with Rebekah, the family’s consent, and the blessing on the departure. Isaac would hear how God had led, step by step, to the woman now standing before him.

That report would have been a powerful testimony. Isaac had been bound on Moriah and spared by God’s provision (22:12–13). Now he learns that the same God has provided him a wife. The God who provided the ram has provided the bride. The servant’s faithful account allowed Isaac to see his marriage as God’s gift, not merely a family arrangement.

The servant’s report is his last act in the story. He has fulfilled his oath and finished his errand. Like the faithful servant in Jesus’ parable, he can give account of his stewardship with a clear conscience (Matthew 25:21). He fades from view without having been named, having served his master and his master’s son with complete loyalty. His reward is the success of his mission and the knowledge that God used him.

wordNotes.explanation: Davar again carries its double sense of “words” and “matters”: the servant recounted everything that had happened. The same summary phrase is used when Moses told Aaron, and later the people, all the LORD’s words, and when Jacob told Laban all that had happened.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter ends with a single verse that brings everything to rest: “Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.” Four short statements describe the marriage, and a fifth describes its effect on Isaac.

First, Isaac brings Rebekah into Sarah’s tent. In a nomadic household the principal wife had her own tent, and Sarah’s had stood empty for three years. By bringing Rebekah into it, Isaac installs her as the new mistress of the household, the successor to Sarah as mother of the promised line. Rebekah has left her “mother’s house” (v. 28) and enters Isaac’s mother’s tent. The circle of the story closes: it opened with Abraham old and bereaved, and it ends with a new household established in the place Sarah left.

Second, he “took Rebekah, and she became his wife.” The marriage was probably sealed simply, with the bride brought into the husband’s dwelling before witnesses. No elaborate ceremony is described. What matters is that God’s purpose has been fulfilled: the son of promise has a wife from the right family, a woman of faith who chose to come.

Third, “he loved her.” This is the first time Scripture says a man loved his wife. Isaac’s love is mentioned after the marriage, not before. The order reflects the way love grew in many arranged marriages: commitment came first, and affection deepened within it. Yet the statement is warm and personal. The marriage God arranged was not a cold contract. Isaac loved Rebekah, and that love would endure through twenty years of barrenness (25:20–21) and many trials. Paul calls husbands to love their wives “even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Ephesians 5:25). Isaac’s love for Rebekah is a small human picture of that greater love.

Finally, “Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.” Isaac had been mourning Sarah for three years. Rebekah’s arrival brought healing to his grief. God’s gift of a wife met not only the needs of the covenant line but the personal sorrow of a lonely son. God cares for both the large purposes of history and the private sorrows of individual hearts. The God who sees, whose well Isaac had visited, saw his grief and sent comfort. The chapter that began with an old man’s concern for the future ends with a young couple’s love. Through prayer, providence, and the free choices of faithful people, God has carried his promise into the next generation.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb ’ahav, “to love,” used here for the first time of a husband’s love for his wife. Earlier it described Abraham’s love for Isaac (22:2). Jacob’s love for Rachel and Elkanah’s for Hannah follow. The note of love within an arranged marriage shows that God’s choice and human affection belong together.

The reflexive form of nacham means to be consoled or to find relief after grief. Jacob “refused to be comforted” over Joseph, and the LORD promises to comfort his people as a mother comforts her child. Isaac’s comfort comes through the gift of a wife.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How does God guide people when he does not speak from heaven or work a visible miracle?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The LORD keeps his covenant promise by leading those who pray and act faithfully, and he invites each person, like Rebekah, to choose freely to follow where the promise goes.
discussionQuestions: Why was Abraham so firm that Isaac must not marry a Canaanite and must not return to Mesopotamia?
What does the servant’s sign at the well reveal about the qualities he was looking for?
How does the servant’s retelling of the story to Rebekah’s family differ from the narrator’s account, and why?
What does Rebekah’s “I will go” have in common with Abraham’s departure in Genesis 12?
Where in your own experience have you recognized God’s leading only after taking a step of obedience?
commonMisunderstandings: The servant’s sign is not a model for demanding arbitrary omens; it tested character and was offered in submission to God’s purpose.
Abraham’s insistence on a wife from his kindred was about shared faith and the covenant, not ethnic pride.
An arranged marriage did not mean Rebekah had no voice; the story makes her consent decisive.
Laban’s use of the LORD’s name does not prove a heart devoted to him; his later conduct shows mixed motives.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep God’s hidden leading and human responsibility together: the servant prays, plans, watches, speaks wisely, and refuses delay, and through these ordinary acts the LORD shows his steadfast love.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Bring your decisions to the God who led Abraham’s servant, act faithfully in the light you have, and be ready to say with Rebekah, “I will go.”

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The faithful God guides those who trust him and calls each person to a free decision to leave the old life and follow him toward the promised inheritance.
flow: God made promises to Abraham that reached beyond his lifetime and centred on a promised Seed.
The LORD showed his steadfast love by guiding a praying servant to the right place at the right moment.
Rebekah heard the message and was asked whether she would go with this man to a land she had never seen.
She answered without delay, “I will go,” and entered the family of promise.
God still calls people to decide to follow Christ and share the inheritance he has promised.
simpleIllustrations: A guide sent to bring someone home can explain the way and show credentials, but the traveller must still choose to set out.
Looking back over a journey, a traveller can often see how each turn led to the destination, though at the time only the next step was clear.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: God has made his love and his promises known to you; will you answer as Rebekah did, “I will go”?
cautions: Do not turn the servant’s sign into a formula for testing God in every decision.
Do not press the allegory of servant, bride, and son beyond what the text itself teaches.
Do not present an arranged marriage as removing personal consent or love.

reflectionQuestions: Do I pray about my plans before I act, and do I give thanks when I see God’s hand in the outcome?
In my choice of friends and especially of a life partner, how much weight do I give to shared faith?
Like the servant, do I put the errand God has given me ahead of my own comfort?
Where is God calling me to leave something familiar and go where his promise leads?
When have I recognized God’s leading only after I had taken a step of trust?
